title: This Thanksgiving, Be Thankful for Forgetting
subtitle: This semester, I’m teaching a hybrid class that only meets on Thursdays.

articleBody:
*By Megan Sumeracki*

This semester, I’m teaching a hybrid class that only meets on Thursdays. Because of this, we have met every week up until this week. However, with Thanksgiving break, my students will have a two-week gap right at the end of the semester. We will return from Thanksgiving break in early December, with the final exam looming around the corner.

These are particularly extreme circumstances, and some students will only have a few days off this holiday. Still, it’s common to come back from Thanksgiving break to hear “I can’t remember.” Or, even more concerning, the “wait, when did we learn this?” question.

As a cognitive psychologist specializing in learning, I’m not overly concerned. It’s counterintuitive, but forgetting is actually an extremely important part of remembering. It’s easier to understand why when we consider how forgetting occurs over time, and how spaced practice works.

In the 1880s, Hermann Ebbinghaus mapped the forgetting curve *(1)*. He showed that forgetting tends to happen very rapidly at first, and then slows down. He also showed that spreading out repetitions was more efficient than massing them, or cramming. We know from a wealth of research in the last 140 years that spaced practice slows the rate of forgetting. This research has confirmed, many times over, that cramming does not work in the long run. Instead, spacing practice leads to much more durable long-term learning and remembering *(2)*.

Why does spacing help? When we review information after some time has passed, it has started to fade. When we revisit the information—or better yet, when we retrieve the information—it takes effort. That effort is sometimes called a desirable difficulty, and it helps produce durable learning *(3)*. Each time we successfully retrieve something, it becomes easier to retrieve the next time, and it is forgotten more slowly afterward. In other words, a little forgetting sets the stage for more durable remembering.

Having a break for Thanksgiving provides a natural space to let students forget a little bit, and then give them a boost upon returning. The figure below shows curves that illustrate the general pattern reported in research on forgetting (e.g., *1, 2* ).

These curves are a simulation, not real data. They illustrate the general pattern reported in research on forgetting and spacing (Ebbinghaus, 1885/1913; Cepeda et al., 2006): memories fade over time, retrieving them brings them back, and each retrieval slows forgetting. The specific values were chosen for illustration and are not predictions.

There are other benefits too. Spacing out practice shifts the context in which the material is being practiced, which may also help produce durable learning and remembering *(4)*. It is also important to take breaks in general. Stress can tax our cognitive resources and make it harder for us to retrieve what we know *(5, 6)*. Sleep also plays an important role in consolidating new memories. If the break provides opportunities to catch up on sleep and destress, it can be beneficial for learning upon return as well. See this post on [The Importance of Sleep for Memory and Cognition](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2016/7/14-1) and this post, [When Do the 6 Strategies for Effective Learning Work Best?](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2017/4/20-1)

Of course, there is a limit to how much space we should put in between review or retrieval attempts. If the space is too long, and the information is completely forgotten, then students may need to relearn it. Likely there will be savings in relearning—i.e., it won’t take as long to learn it again as it did the first time *(1)*. However, the benefits from spaced practice will likely be much less than they would have been, or possibly eliminated. The goal is to retrieve or at least review older material before it is completely forgotten to get the boost. Check out this post, [Optimizing Your Learning Schedule](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2018/7/5-1), to learn more about this.

## What to Do When You Return from Break?

**Teachers**, open the first class after break with a few minutes of low-stakes retrieval before reviewing or moving on. Try a quick “brain dump” or a few big-picture, ungraded questions. You can use what students can’t remember to target any review, and the students will get a boost from the spaced retrieval practice.

**Students**, remember that effort is a good thing. Try to recall from your memory first. Then, and only then, check your notes, ask your teacher, etc. In addition, retrieval may help your memory hold up under exam stress (see [this post on retrieval practice and stress](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2026/3/19)).

**Parents**, you can help by asking your child to explain one thing they have learned this fall. Having them describe and explain in their own words is additional practice. But remember, we do want to let them take the space to forget a bit before revisiting. So, skip any excessive quizzing and encourage your kids to take a restful break.

Enjoy the break, let a little forgetting happen, and come back ready to remember. Happy Thanksgiving!

**References**

(1) Ebbinghaus, H. (1913). *Memory: A contribution to experimental psychology* (H. A. Ruger & C. E. Bussenius, Trans.). Teachers College, Columbia University. (Original work published 1885)

(2) Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. *Psychological Bulletin, 132* (3), 354–380. [https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354](https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354)

(3) Bjork, E. L., & Bjork, R. A. (2011). Making things hard on yourself, but in a good way: Creating desirable difficulties to enhance learning. In M. A. Gernsbacher, R. W. Pew, L. M. Hough, & J. R. Pomerantz (Eds.), *Psychology and the real world: Essays illustrating fundamental contributions to society* (pp. 56–64). Worth Publishers.

(4) Smith, S. M., Glenberg, A., & Bjork, R. A. (1978). Environmental context and human memory. *Memory & Cognition, 6* (4), 342–353. [https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03197465](https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.3758/BF03197465)

(5) Shields, G. S., Sazma, M. A., & Yonelinas, A. P. (2016). title: KOMMENTAR: Abitur 2027 – warum „Sprache in politisch-gesellschaftlichen Verwendungszusammenhängen“ in jede Oberstufe gehört
subtitle: Kaum ein Abiturthema zeigt so deutlich wie dieses, dass es ihn gibt: einen modernen Deutschunterricht, der die Aufgabe ernst nimmt, jungen Menschen…

articleBody:
Kaum ein Abiturthema zeigt so deutlich wie dieses, dass es ihn gibt: einen modernen Deutschunterricht, der die Aufgabe ernst nimmt, jungen Menschen Orientierung in einer digitalen Gesellschaft zu ermöglichen. Ein Kommentar.

Es gibt Abiturthemen, bei denen man als Lehrkraft erst einmal Überzeugungsarbeit leisten muss. Bei denen man vor einem Kurs steht und begründen muss, warum es sich lohnt, sich mit etwas zu beschäftigen, das auf den ersten Blick weit weg ist vom eigenen Leben. Ich habe solche Stunden oft genug gehalten. Und ich habe auf diesem Blog auch schon [dafür gestritten, dass man sie halten sollte.](https://bobblume.de/2019/10/06/diskussion-sollte-goethes-faust-teil-des-lehrplans-sein/)

„Sprache in politisch-gesellschaftlichen Verwendungszusammenhängen“ gehört nicht dazu. Der sperrige Titel täuscht. Denn worum es hier geht, tragen die Schülerinnen und Schüler jeden Tag in der Hosentasche mit sich herum.

## Wo das Thema im Abitur 2027 eine Rolle spielt

In Nordrhein-Westfalen, Berlin und Brandenburg, Hessen, Niedersachsen und Schleswig-Holstein ist das Themenfeld im Abitur 2027 ausdrücklich als Schwerpunkt ausgewiesen, mit leicht unterschiedlichen Akzenten. Mal geht es um politisch-gesellschaftliche Kommunikation zwischen Verständigung und Strategie, mal um den Sprachgebrauch in unterschiedlichen Medien, mal um Rhetorik und Medienwandel. In den übrigen Ländern, etwa in Baden-Württemberg und Bayern, sind genau die Aufgabenformate gefragt, an denen sich das Thema hervorragend üben lässt: die Analyse pragmatischer Texte, die Erörterung und das materialgestützte Schreiben.

Mit anderen Worten: Es ist eines der zentralen Felder des Deutschabiturs.

## Worum es eigentlich geht

Wie wird Sprache eingesetzt, um zu überzeugen, zu mobilisieren, auszugrenzen? Wo legt jemand seine Gründe offen, und wo will er bloß wirken? Diese Fragen konnte man früher an Bundestagsreden und Leitartikeln stellen. Das fällt nicht weg, aber es kommt auch etwas hinzu: Die politisch-gesellschaftliche Kommunikation, die Jugendliche tatsächlich erreicht, hat nochmals völlig andere Formen und Kanäle: ein KI-generiertes Video, das Empörung erzeugt und am Ende einen Shop verlinkt. Ein [Finanzpodcast, der von „Systemmedien“](https://www.t-online.de/leben/kolumne-bob-blume/id_100330412/finanz-influencer-und-podcasts-werden-jugendliche-zum-rechtsruck-verleitet-.html) spricht und damit mehr transportiert als eine Meinung. Eine Kommentarspalte, in der niemand den Text gelesen hat, über den alle streiten. Ein Feed, in dem auf das Kriegsvideo der Tanzclip folgt.

Das ist politische Sprache. Nur eben nicht mehr im Plenarsaal, sondern zwischen zwei Wischbewegungen. Und wer diese Sprache nicht durchschaut, wird von ihr beeinflusst oder [im schlimmsten Fall manipuliert.](https://substack.com/@netzlehrer/p-211289258)

## Kein Entweder-oder

Nun könnte man einwenden, das sei die übliche Anbiederung an die Lebenswelt. Ein bisschen TikTok, damit es sich zeitgemäß anfühlt. Den Einwand muss man ernst nehmen, ich habe ihn selbst oft genug erhoben. An anderer Stelle habe ich beschrieben, dass Deutschunterricht auf [drei Ebenen zur Teilhabe an Kultur](https://bobblume.de/2021/05/31/diskussion-was-soll-und-kann-deutschunterricht/) befähigt: durch basale Grundfertigkeiten, durch die Auseinandersetzung mit Alltagskultur und durch die Hochkultur. Die mittlere Ebene ist diejenige, die sich am schnellsten verändert. Gerade deshalb darf man sie nicht dem Zufall überlassen.

Und es geht nicht um ein Entweder-oder. Wer Kleist liest, lernt etwas über Macht und Sprache vor Gericht. Wer ein Empörungsvideo analysiert, lernt etwas über Macht und Sprache im Feed. Beides schärft denselben Blick. In der Diskussion um den Faust habe ich geschrieben, dass man Kompetenzen an unterschiedlichen Inhalten lernen kann, aber nur an bestimmten Inhalten unterschiedliche Kompetenzen. Die Sprache der digitalen Öffentlichkeit ist ein solcher Inhalt. An ihr lernt man zu analysieren, zu urteilen und selbst zu schreiben. Und nebenbei etwas, das in keinem Erwartungshorizont steht: den Schritt zurück.

## Fazit

Man kann lange darüber streiten, wie viel Gegenwart der Deutschunterricht verträgt. Bei diesem Thema muss man es nicht. Wenn Schule der Ort sein soll, an dem junge Menschen lernen, sich in der Welt zu orientieren, dann muss sie sich mit der Sprache beschäftigen, in der diese Welt heute verhandelt wird. Nicht obwohl sie den Schülerinnen und Schülern so nah ist, sondern weil sie es ist. Relevanz ist hier kein Zugeständnis an die Jugend. Sie ist der Grund, warum das Thema in die Schule gehört.

## Unterrichtseinheit

**Abitur 2027: Sprache in Politik und Gesellschaft – analysieren, erörtern und materialgestützt schreiben mit echten Kolumnen**

Wie funktioniert politisch-gesellschaftliche Kommunikation im Netz? Dieses Abiturpaket bereitet Grund- und Leistungskurse auf den Schwerpunkt „Sprache in politisch-gesellschaftlichen Verwendungszusammenhängen“ vor. Es arbeitet mit echten Kolumnen, die auf WEB.DE und t-online erschienen sind: über Empörungsvideos, radikale Influencer, „Decline Porn“, Kommentarkultur, KI und soziale Medien. Dazu kommt ein wissenschaftlicher Essay als theoretischer Rahmen. Alle Texte sind rechtssicher einsetzbar.

[Zum Material- und Unterrichtspaket](https://eduki.com/de/material/2478468/abiturpaket-2027-sprache-in-politik-und-gesellschaft-1)

## In eigener Sache

Vielleicht ist es euch aufgefallen: Auf diesem Blog war es in letzter Zeit ruhiger. Das liegt nicht daran, dass mir die Themen ausgegangen wären, sondern daran, dass ich vor allem auf Substack schreibe. Dort erscheint jeden Samstag mein Newsletter „Stimme für Bildungswandel“, mit Kommentaren zu Bildungsthemen, Gesprächen und regelmäßig auch mit Material für den Unterricht. Wenn ihr mögt, schaut dort gern vorbei. Die Anmeldung ist kostenlos.

title: Listen to the Music of the Ancient World: From 40,000-Year-Old Flutes to Ancient Greek Songs
subtitle: There aren’t many ways to experience the ancient world.

articleBody:
There aren’t many ways to experience the ancient world. We can learn its languages, at least the ones that have left behind decipherable writings; we can behold its artifacts; we can visit its ruins. But nothing gets us quite as close to entering the consciousness of our distant forebears as hearing the music — or at least the sounds — that they did. In [the new Archaeologist’s Notebook video above](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2nWf_OXdKz8), Giselle Király gives us a tour through ancient musical history, explaining the instruments of those times that survive in one form or another today. That tour begins at a much earlier point than many would expect: 40,000 years ago, in the depths of the last Ice Age, when humans were already punctuating their struggle for survival with organized sound.

As evidence, Király points to the “tiny, exquisitely crafted flutes carved from animal bone and mammoth ivory” discovered on cave floors around Europe. Surprisingly, when played in replica form, these vulture- or swan-bone flutes actually sound somewhat Middle Eastern. But whatever the stylistic traits of the music their original players produced, that music had the potential to confer benefits beyond immediate pleasure: “It would’ve connected people, built cohesion within the community,” and maybe even bridged “the land of the living with some spiritual world.” Each of the other discovered or reconstructed instruments, like swingable “bullroarers,” bone rasps, and lithophones (of the kind [previously featured here on Open Culture](https://www.openculture.com/2019/09/watch-an-archaeologist-play-the-lithophone.html)) would have played its own sonic part to that end.

Király also discusses the lavishly decorated Lyres of Ur, the world’s oldest surviving stringed instruments; a 3,500-year-old Egyptian long-necked lute with a guitar-like fingerboard; and a set of 65 Chinese *bianzhong * bells covering a five-octave range. But music isn’t just about the objects it’s played with. Also important are the means of recording it, an ancient example of which Király cites in the [Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal](https://www.openculture.com/2023/03/hear-the-oldest-song-in-the-world-a-sumerian-hymn-written-3400-years-ago.html) inscribed on a clay tablet around 1400 BC, the oldest known complete musical notation. Centuries later, in the Greek-speaking world — and in the more monumental form of a marble stele — a man named Seikilos recorded an epitaph to which we now refer by his name. The lyrics of this [oldest completely preserved, fully playable musical composition](https://www.openculture.com/2015/05/hear-the-seikilos-epitaph-the-oldest-complete-song-in-the-world.html) exhort the listener: “While you live, shine. Have no grief at all.” For “life exists only for a short while,” and “time demands its toll.” The ancients needed to hear this no less, perhaps, than we do.

# Crucifix with Scenes of the Passion | Cleveland Museum of Art

## Artwork Page for Crucifix with Scenes of the Passion

### Details / Information for Crucifix with Scenes of the Passion

### Crucifix with Scenes of the Passion

c. 1230–40

#### Italy, Pisa

Mediumtempera with gold on panelMeasurementsFramed: 186.6 x 160.7 x 12.7 cm (73 7/16 x 63 1/4 x 5 in.); Unframed: 185 x 160 x 10.2 cm (72 13/16 x 63 x 4 in.)Credit LineLeonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund 1995.5You can copy, modify, and distribute this work, all without asking permission. Learn more about CMA's Open Access Initiative.Location100 1916 LobbyArtLens AppPrint?

#### Did You Know?

Although the artist did sign this panel at the bottom, the signature is illegible, his first name perhaps being Michael.

### Description

Large painted crucifixes dating from the 1100s and 1200s are among the earliest surviving Italian panel paintings. Large crosses, like this beautiful example, were typically suspended high above an altar in the main apse of Italian churches. Smaller crosses were placed on or just above altars in small side chapels. Such crosses served as the visual focus for devotion and symbolized the Eucharistic sacrament performed by the priest on the altar below. This crucifix shows Christ alive on the cross as the triumphant savior of mankind. Smaller images on the "apron" represent images of Christ's Passion (to the left) and his death and Resurrection (to the right). On the far left terminal appear the mourning Virgin and Saint John the Evangelist, while on the right the viewer is shown Saint James Major and Saint Bona, patroness of the city of Pisa. The concluding event, the Ascension of Christ, once appeared on the upper terminal, just above the Virgin and Apostles. The figure of Christ is painted in a severe and hieratic style suggestive of medieval Pisa's artistic and commercial links with the Byzantine East. The appearance of Saint Bona on this cross may suggest that it was made for the Church of S. Martino in Pisa, where Franciscan nuns tended the holy woman's relics.

### Crucifix with Scenes of the Passion

c. 1230–40

Italy, Pisa

articleBody:
### “A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader.”

*“All attempts at gaining literary polish must begin with judicious reading,”* H.P. Lovecraft [advised aspiring writers](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/01/11/h-p-lovecraft-advice-on-writing/). We’ve already seen that [reading is a learned skill](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/01/09/best-books-on-writing-reading/) and an [optimizable technique](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/01/16/how-to-read-faster-bill-cosby/), and that [non-reading](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/06/15/how-to-talk-about-books-you-havent-read/) is as important an intellectual choice as reading itself, so it follows that reading, more than the mere monolithic act of ingesting text, comes with degrees of mastery. But what, exactly, does it mean to be a *good* reader?

**Vladimir Nabokov** (April 22, 1899–July 2, 1977) was a man of [wonderfully opinionated insights on literature and life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/01/18/vladimir-nabokov-james-mossman-interview/). He was also, it turns out, equally opinionated in his criteria for what constitutes a good reader. In his collected [Lectures on Literature](http://www.amazon.com/Lectures-Literature-Vladimir-Nabokov/dp/0156027755/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/lectures-on-literature/oclc/6357239&referer=brief_results)), Nabokov offers the following exercise, which he posed to students at a “remote provincial college” while on an extended lecture tour:

> Select four answers to the question what should a reader be to be a good reader:
> The reader should belong to a book club.
> The reader should identify himself or herself with the hero or heroine.
> The reader should concentrate on the social-economic angle.
> The reader should prefer a story with action and dialogue to one with none.
> The reader should have seen the book in a movie.
> The reader should be a budding author.
> The reader should have imagination.
> The reader should have memory.
> The reader should have a dictionary.
> The reader should have some artistic sense.
> The students leaned heavily on emotional identification, action, and the social-economic or historical angle. Of course, as you have guessed, the good reader is one who has imagination, memory, a dictionary, and some artistic sense–which sense I propose to develop in myself and in others whenever I have the chance.

He goes on to consider the element of time in reading, making a case for the value of rereading:

> Incidentally, I use the word reader very loosely. Curiously enough, one cannot read a book: one can only reread it. A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader. And I shall tell you why. When we read a book for the first time the very process of laboriously moving our eyes from left to right, line after line, page after page, this complicated physical work upon the book, the very process of learning in terms of space and time what the book is about, this stands between us and artistic appreciation. When we look at a painting we do not have to move our eyes in a special way even if, as in a book, the picture contains elements of depth and development. The element of time does not really enter in a first contact with a painting. In reading a book, we must have time to acquaint ourselves with it. We have no physical organ (as we have the eye in regard to a painting) that takes in the whole picture and then can enjoy its details. But at a second, or third, or fourth reading we do, in a sense, behave towards a book as we do towards a painting. However, let us not confuse the physical eye, that monstrous masterpiece of evolution, with the mind, an even more monstrous achievement. A book, no matter what it is—a work of fiction or a work of science (the boundary line between the two is not as clear as is generally believed)—a book of fiction appeals first of all to the mind. The mind, the brain, the top of the tingling spine, is, or should be, the only instrument used upon a book.

Complement with Mark Twain’s humorous list of [the fourteen types of readers](https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/06/13/mark-twain-nypl-flash-rosenberg/) and Nabokov on [the three qualities a great storyteller must have](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/02/21/vladimir-nabokov-on-storytelling/).

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

articleBody:
**STUTTGART. „Vielfalt stärken – Zukunft gestalten“ lautete das Motto des Jahreskongresses Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026, zu dem am 26./27. November in der IHK Region Stuttgart rund 400 Ausbilder:innen, Schulleitungen und Lehrkräfte zusammenkamen.**

Dr. Christoph Franz, Dr. Benny Pock, Andrea Bosch, Dr. Jens Brandenburg und Andreas Deuschle beim Jahreskongress Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026. (Foto © Laurenz Bostedt für Klett MEX)

Mit **Andreas Deuschle, Staatssekretär im Ministerium für Kultus Baden-Württemberg**, wurde heute der Jahreskongress Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026 in Stuttgart eröffnet. Deuschle vertrat Kultusminister Andreas Jung, der in diesem Jahr erstmals die Schirmherrschaft des Kongresses übernommen hat. Jung bezeichnete die berufliche Bildung kürzlich in einem Interview als „Flaggschiff“, „Aushängeschild“ und eine Basis des wirtschaftlichen Erfolges seines Bundeslandes. Entsprechend wurde auf die duale Ausbildung im Koalitionsvertrag von BÜNDNIS 90/DIE GRÜNEN und CDU ein besonderer Schwerpunkt gesetzt. Im Begrüßungsgespräch mit der stellvertretenden Hauptgeschäftsführerin der IHK Region Stuttgart, Andrea Bosch, ging es darum, wie das Kultusministerium dieses Vorhaben gemeinsam mit dem Wirtschaftsministerium in Schulen und Betrieben mit Leben füllen will. Deuschle betonte dabei, dass es gelte, „gemeinsam Perspektiven zu schaffen“.

**Austausch über Zuständigkeiten hinweg**

Dass diese politische Zielsetzung nur gemeinsam gelingen kann, spiegelte das Teilnehmerfeld des jakobb 2026 wider: Als Plattform für die berufliche Bildung versammelt der Kongress einmal im Jahr alle Schlüsselakteure an einem Ort. Von der Berufsschullehrkraft bis zur Personalleitung mittelständischer und globaler Unternehmen nutzten die Entscheidungsträger den Austausch in Stuttgart, um Weichen für die Ausbildung von morgen zu stellen.

**Dr. Christoph Franz**, Vorsitzender des Berufsschullehrerverbands Baden-Württemberg (BLV), und Mitveranstalter des jakobb, zum Konzept: „ Wir erleben täglich, unter welchem Druck die berufliche Bildung steht: Fachkräftemangel, Transformation der Wirtschaft, Digitalisierung und KI, Integration und zunehmend heterogene Klassen. Diese Aufgaben kann niemand allein lösen. Der jakobb bringt Lehrkräfte, Schulleitungen, Wirtschaft, Verwaltung und Wissenschaft an einen Tisch. Genau diesen Austausch über Zuständigkeiten hinweg brauchen wir jetzt. Gleichzeitig zeigt der jakobb, was die beruflichen Schulen in Baden-Württemberg leisten. Sie sind kein Plan B, sondern ein Erfolgsmodell und das Rückgrat der Fachkräftesicherung im Land.“

Der jakobb bringt die Akteure der beruflichen Bildung miteinander ins Gespräch. (Foto © Laurenz Bostedt für Klett MEX)

**Raus aus dem Tagungsraum, rein in die Praxis**

Ein weiteres Alleinstellungsmerkmal des Kongresses ist die konsequente Verbindung von Theorie und Praxis: Wenn die Fachvorträge und Diskussionsrunden enden, öffnen regelmäßig am zweiten Veranstaltungstag Spitzenunternehmen sowie innovative berufsbildende Schulen in der Region Stuttgart ihre Türen für exklusive „jakobb-Führungen“. **Dr. Benny Pock**, Geschäftsführer von Klett MEX und Mitgründer des jakobb, unterstreicht die Bedeutung dieses Formats: „ Der jakobb belässt es nicht beim theoretischen Diskurs. Unser Ziel war von Anfang an, die beiden Lernorte der dualen Ausbildung – den betrieblichen und den schulischen Teil – nicht nur an einen Tisch zu bringen, sondern vor Ort erlebbar zu machen. Die Exkursionen bieten Ausbildungsverantwortlichen und Lehrkräften die Chance, voneinander zu lernen, Best Practices im laufenden Betrieb zu studieren und frische Impulse direkt in die eigene Ausbildungspraxis mitzunehmen.“

Das Spektrum der Exkursionsziele, die in diesem Jahr ausgewählt wurden, spiegelt die wirtschaftliche und schulische Vielfalt der Region Stuttgart wider. Bei den Technologieführern ANDREAS STIHL AG & Co. KG in Waiblingen, der Siemens AG, der Festo SE & Co. KG sowie der Schnaithmann Maschinenbau GmbH in Remshalden erhielten die Teilnehmenden direkte Einblicke in hochmoderne Ausbildungswerkstätten, automatisierte Produktionsstraßen und zukunftsweisende Lehrkonzepte rund um Digitalisierung und KI. Auf schulischer Seite präsentierten die Gottlieb-Daimler-Schule 2 in Sindelfingen, die gewerbliche Max-Eyth-Schule Stuttgart und das GARP Bildungszentrum in Plochingen Einblicke in moderne Ausbildungsstätten und zukunftsfähige Unterrichtskonzepte.

**Prominente Impulse, Fachmesse und vier Praxis-Vortragsrunden**

Fabian Hambüchen im Gespräch mit Dr. Benny Pock (Foto © Laurenz Bostedt für Klett MEX)

Am ersten Kongresstag bot der jakobb 2026 neben den Hauptvorträgen und Talks – etwa von Olympiasieger **Fabian Hambüchen**zur Übertragbarkeit von mentaler Stärke aus dem Leistungssport auf den Schul- und Ausbildungsalltag sowie von**HR-Expertin Felicitas von Kyaw** zu zukunftsfähigen Skillsets in einer dynamischen Arbeitswelt – ein gewohnt dichtes Fachprogramm. In insgesamt vier Vortragsrunden mit parallel laufenden Sessions erarbeiteten die Teilnehmenden konkrete Lösungsansätze für den Praxisalltag. Das Themenspektrum reichte dabei von Lernortkooperationen über Handlungsleitfäden für mentale Gesundheit und Krisen-Ersthilfe bis hin zu modernen Onboarding-Konzepten und Stellschrauben im Umgang mit Neurodivergenz. Abgerundet wurde die Veranstaltung durch eine begleitende Fachmesse, auf der sich die Besucherinnen und Besucher direkt vor Ort mit innovativen Anbietern und Partnern der beruflichen Bildung vernetzen konnten.

Die Termine für die nächsten jakobb-Events stehen bereits fest: Am 6. und 7. Dezember 2027 trifft sich das „Who’s who der beruflichen Bildung“ erneut in der IHK Region Stuttgart. Bereits am 4. und 5. Mai 2027 findet die zweite Auflage des Berliner jakobb-Ablegers gemeinsam mit dem Christiani Ausbildertag statt. Den Ticketshop und weitere Informationen findet man unter [www.jakobb.de](http://www.jakobb.de)

*Eine Meldung der Klett MEX GmbH.*

**Über Klett MEX** Die Klett MEX GmbH ist ein Unternehmen der Klett Gruppe. Das Leistungsspektrum der Stuttgarter Full-Service-Agentur umfasst die drei Kernfelder „Beraten“, „Entwickeln“ sowie „Vernetzen & Vermarkten“. Für Stiftungen, Ministerien, Unternehmen, Verbände, Hochschulen und NGOs setzt Klett MEX innovative Bildungsprojekte um. Zu wichtigen Bildungsthemen und -bereichen hat die Agentur eigene Marken aufgebaut und fungiert damit als Impulsgeber, Orientierungsstifter und Vernetzer. 2026 wurde das Portfolio in der Bildungskommunikation unter der neuen Marke jungvornweg by Klett MEX gezielt um Formate erweitert, die Kinder, Jugendliche und die GenZ direkt adressieren und aktiv einbeziehen.

Um den Neustart der beruflichen Bildung aktiv mitzugestalten, hatt Klett MEX 2015 den Jahreskongress Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) ins Leben gerufen. Das innovative Praxis-Event bringt mit einem Mix aus Kongress, Fachmesse und Exkursionsprogramm die betriebliche und die schulische Seite der Dualen Ausbildung miteinander ins Gespräch. Veranstalter sind die Klett MEX GmbH, der BLV BW und das Bundesinstitut für Berufsbildung (BIBB) in enger Kooperation mit der IHK Region Stuttgart sowie dem Didacta Verband e. V.. Neben Stuttgart ist der Kongress seit 2026 auch in Berlin vertreten und bietet darüber hinaus ganzjährig digitale Veranstaltungsformate an.

articleBody:
# Intellectual telescopes

This is a post from Robin Sloan’s lab blog & notebook. You can visit the blog’s homepage, or learn more about me.

## Intellectual telescopes

November 25, 2026

In a pre­vious post, I tried out an analogy for AI-assisted work: the pantograph, a once-ubiquitous tool for trans­forming human draw­ings vastly larger or minutely smaller, allowing human-sized hands to per­form nimbly at dif­ferent scales.

Here’s another analogy from the com­ments sec­tion on Scott Aaronson’s blog:

In any case, I recently saw this num­ber­phile video on the Rie­mann hypoth­esis with Jon Keating. At some point, Brady asks him some­thing like “Is it pos­sible that the proof of the Rie­mann hypoth­esis is some­thing that no human can understand, that our hardware, our brains, just can’t process?”

And Keating replies “Yes, that is pos­sible. Humans have faced this before. If I want to see the stars, I would quite like to see them with my own eyes. But there are cer­tain things in the uni­verse that the Hubble space tele­scope can see that my eyes can’t see. And I am pre­pared to accept that the Hubble space tele­scope does a better job than my eyes. And I just look at the pic­tures it pro­duces, in wonderment”.

I like this a lot. Although, it’s impor­tant to say the formal math lan­guage Lean is as much “the space tele­scope” here as the AI lan­guage models; they wouldn’t be able to pro­duce any­thing leg­ible or ver­i­fi­able without it.

Finally, it strikes me that this kind of work is very impor­tant — it’s the equiv­a­lent of actu­ally ren­dering space tele­scope “images” (which are just streams of numbers) into pic­tures, very prob­ably false-colored, that humans can con­sider and appreciate.

P.S. Of course, you could also use another analogy, emphasis mine …

As long as there are prob­lems to solve, and as long as we bring some­thing to their resolution, I think we should ride the AI dragon. We should enhance ourselves, move up in abstraction, and let the dragon deal with what it does better than us. [ … ]

I doubt that riding the dragon can be a pro­gram for the steady-state ASI sce­nario (if there is one), but it can be a pro­gram for now. The dragon is get­ting bigger every three months. It may ride itself at some point, but so far few can ride it properly. Those who do not ride it now may never be able to ride it in the future, at least not to find new things.

… which, from the title of this blog, you already know I love🤓

title: Was zehn Jahre Wissenschaftskommunikation.de verändert haben
subtitle: Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten.
feedText: Annette Leßmöllmann und Markus Weißkopf sprechen zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de über Erfolge, Herausforderungen und notwendigen Wandel. Am 24. November 2016 ging Wissenschaftskommunikation.de online. In unserem Schwerpunkt zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum blicken wir auf prägende Entwicklungen zurück und fragen, wo die Wissenschaftskommunikation heute steht. Mit welcher Idee und welchem persönlichen Anspruch seid Ihr 2016 an der Gründung von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de beteiligt gewesen?…
articleBody:
Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten. Annette Leßmöllmann und Markus Weißkopf sprechen zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de über Erfolge, Herausforderungen und notwendigen Wandel.

Am 24. November 2016 ging Wissenschaftskommunikation.de online. In unserem [Schwerpunkt zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wo-steht-die-wisskomm/)blicken wir auf prägende Entwicklungen zurück *und fragen, wo die Wissenschaftskommunikation heute steht.*

**Mit welcher Idee und welchem persönlichen Anspruch seid Ihr 2016 an der Gründung von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de beteiligt gewesen?**

**Markus Weißkopf** ist Redakteur des Research.Table bei Table.Media. Er war Geschäftsführer von Wissenschaft im Dialog und hat dort unter anderem die Plattform Wissenschaftskommunikation.de aufgebaut. Foto: WiD

Markus Weißkopf: Kurz zuvor hatten Wissenschaft im Dialog und der Bundesverband Hochschulkommunikation gemeinsam die [Leitlinien zur guten Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/leitlinien-zur-guten-wissenschaftskommunikation-85129/) veröffentlicht. In dem Zuge hatte die Community viel über gemeinsame Werte, aber auch über die Professionalisierung der Wissenschaftskommunikation diskutiert. Wissenschaftskommunikation.de sollte unter anderem eine Plattform für diese Themen bieten.

Annette Leßmöllmann: Die Plattform sollte zeigen: Wissenschaftskommunikation bedeutet mehr als nur Pressemitteilungen und Hochglanzmagazine. Mir war es ein Anliegen, Forschung und Praxis zusammenzubringen und somit die [Vermittlung der Wissenschaftskommunikationsforschung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/kategorie/forschung/) voranzutreiben. Zum einen, um praxisrelevante Ergebnisse bekannt zu machen, zum anderen, um die theoretische Weiterentwicklung, die Interdisziplinarität und die Selbstreflexion des Forschungsfeldes zu zeigen. Gleichzeitig sollten Praxisfragen für die Forschung nachvollziehbar werden, um neue Forschung anzustoßen.

**Annette Leßmöllmann** (@annetteless.bsky.social) ist promovierte Linguistin und hat am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT)* den Lehrstuhl für Wissenschaftskommunikation mit dem Schwerpunkt Linguistik inne. Sie lehrt in den Bachelor- und Master-Studiengängen „Wissenschaft – Medien – Kommunikation“ (@WMKstudium).

**Welche Fragen oder Konfliktlinien aus der Gründungszeit beschäftigen die Community bis heute?**

Weißkopf: „Als Anlaufstelle Nr. 1 hat sich das Online-Lexikon Wikipedia im Internet längst etabliert. Die Wissenschaft sollte das Potenzial von Wikipedia für die Vermittlung fundierten Wissens ernsthaft prüfen.“ Das hat eine Pressesprecherin [im Rahmen des ersten Schwerpunkts „Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation“](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/blick-nach-vorn-wie-sieht-die-wissenschaftskommunikation-der-zukunft-aus-5-13517/) geschrieben. Natürlich ist das Prüfen wissenschaftsimmanent. Aber im Bereich der Kommunikation können wir es uns nicht erlauben, jahrelang zu prüfen. Die Wissenschaft hat nun ein Engagement bei oder für [Wikipedia](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/format/wikipedia/) so lange geprüft, bis es zu spät war. Nur einzelne Einrichtungen wie die Universität Innsbruck bilden hier Ausnahmen. Da würde ich mir manchmal mehr Mut zum Experimentieren wünschen!

Leßmöllmann: Was sich bereits vor zehn Jahren angekündigt hat: Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden. Dass sie in Interessenslagen und Machtstrukturen eingebettet ist und dass es als machtvoller kommunikativer Akt angesehen wird, wenn jemand „bestimmt“, was wahr oder falsch ist – das war damals eher ein Gedankenexperiment, ist heute aber deutlich als Konflikt zu spüren.

Es wird für die Wissenschaftskommunikation viel schwieriger, wenn es den Entscheider*innen reicht, dass sich etwas wahr anfühlt, auch wenn es nicht wahr ist. Dass etwa politische und gesellschaftliche Entscheidungen gegen den vorherrschenden wissenschaftlichen Konsens getroffen werden, ist angesichts der Klimakrise deutlich bedrohlicher und krisenhafter spürbar als noch vor zehn Jahren.

### „Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden.“

Annette Leßmöllmann

**Direkt mit dem ersten Schwerpunkt des Portals haben wir damals auf die** **[Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/zukunft-der-wissenschaftskommunikation/)** **geblickt. Welche damaligen Hoffnungen und Befürchtungen haben sich aus Eurer Sicht bewahrheitet und welche nicht?**

Leßmöllmann: Es hat sich die Hoffnung bewahrheitet, dass heute stärker darauf geachtet wird, Kommunikationsaktivitäten wissenschaftlich fundiert zu evaluieren. Zudem hat es funktioniert, dass sich die Community intensiver vernetzt und dass Forschung und Praxis enger zusammenarbeiten.

Es gab auch den Wunsch, dass Wissenschaftskommunikation stärker Teil der Gesellschaft und des täglichen Austauschs über die relevanten Themen der Zeit wird. In einem Aspekt hat sich der Wunsch bewahrheitet, allerdings anders als gedacht: Durch [generative Künstliche Intelligenz](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/themen/kuenstliche-intelligenz/) sind Wissen und Wissenschaft jetzt noch einfacher und dialogischer zu erreichen.

Gleichzeitig wurde die DIN-Norm der Kommunikation aufgeweicht: Es ist nicht mehr sicher, ob das Kommunizierte auch stimmt. Dies trägt zu einer Wissenskrise bei. Etwas dystopisch und pointiert formuliert: Gesagt und geglaubt wird, was gut klingt und auf die Interessen der eigenen Peer Group einzahlt. Das zeigt, dass wir in einer völlig anderen Welt als vor zehn Jahren leben. Die Rolle des Wissens, die demokratische Verankerung und die Wissenschaftsfreiheit stehen zur Debatte.

Das Gründungs-Team (ohne Markus Weißkopf) bei der Präsentation der Plattform im Dezember 2016. Thorsten Witt, Esther Kähler, Beatrice Lugger, Annette Leßmöllmann, Christian Humm und Ulrike Brandt-Bohne. Foto: Gesine Born/WiD.

**Was muss gute Wissenschaftskommunikation heute leisten, was bei der Gründung des Portals noch eine deutlich geringere Rolle gespielt hat?**

Weißkopf: Natürlich markierten der Brexit und die Wahl Trumps im Jahr 2016 nochmal eine Beschleunigung des Populismus, doch einige Entwicklungen waren schon abzusehen. Dennoch muss man sagen, dass die Macht der Tech-Konzerne, die autokratischen Tendenzen auch im „alten Westen“ und der Aufstieg der Rechten aus der Perspektive von 2016 ein Worst Case-Szenario darstellen. Dazu kommen der Ukraine-Krieg und die Konflikte im Nahen Osten.

Mit diesem veränderten geopolitischen und Kommunikationsumfeld muss die Wissenschaftskommunikation umgehen: Kann ich noch guten Gewissens auf X sein? Wie spreche ich über China-Kooperationen meiner Einrichtungen? Muss sich meine Einrichtung politisch positionieren? Die [Debatte über ein Verbot von Zivilklauseln](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wer-erklaert-die-bedrohung-sicherheit-als-neue-aufgabe-der-wissenschaftskommunikation-100967/) zeigt exemplarisch, wie sich hier die Diskurse verändert haben.

### „Die Debatte über ein Verbot von Zivilklauseln zeigt exemplarisch, wie sich hier die Diskurse verändert haben.“

Markus Weißkopf

Leßmöllmann: Wenn man an Themen wie [Militär- oder Verteidigungsforschung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/schwerpunkt-sicherheit-innovation/) denkt, die aus Sicherheitsgründen nicht immer öffentlich verhandelt werden können, dürfen oder sollen, wird deutlich, dass die Wissenschaftskommunikation vor Herausforderungen steht, was zum Beispiel Forderungen nach Transparenz und Dialog betrifft.

Auch wird heute deutlicher als noch vor zehn Jahren: Die Geistes- und Sozialwissenschaften sind immens wichtig, da sie Phänomene wie Migration, Demokratieabbau und Polarisierung beschreiben oder sogar erklären können. Heutzutage reicht es jedoch nicht mehr aus, sie sichtbarer zu machen. Man muss sie auch schützen, da sie teilweise mit unerträglichem Hass konfrontiert sind.

**Wo sollten Wissenschaftskommunikation.de und die Wissenschaftskommunikation insgesamt im Jahr 2036 stehen?**

Weißkopf: Wir haben nicht bis zum Jahr 2036 Zeit, um etwas zu ändern. Es geht jetzt darum, wirkungsvolle Wissenschaftskommunikation im Sinne der Leitlinien zu betreiben. Das bedeutet auch, dass man für gemeinsame Ziele den Konkurrenzgedanken beiseitelegen und Kooperationen anstreben sollte. Dafür braucht es Ressourcen für gemeinnützige Kommunikation. Diese können nur von den Leitungen bereitgestellt werden, müssen aber auch von den Kommunikator*innen eingefordert werden.

Leßmöllmann: Ich wünsche mir, dass das Portal als Stimme der Professionalität und des Austauschs zwischen Theorie und Praxis erhalten bleibt – und auch als Anlaufpunkt und Anker in schwierigen Zeiten. Wir betreiben unabhängigen Fachjournalismus und werden international dafür beneidet.

### „Ich wünsche mir, dass das Portal als Stimme der Professionalität und des Austauschs zwischen Theorie und Praxis erhalten bleibt – und auch als Anlaufpunkt und Anker in schwierigen Zeiten.“

Annette Leßmöllmann

Das Portal würde im Jahr 2036 anders aussehen, aber der Spirit wäre derselbe. Wir denken und schreiben selbst (siehe unsere [Policy zur KI-Nutzung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/netiquette/)) und übernehmen die Verantwortung dafür, dass wir die Forschungs- und Praxislandschaft qualifiziert beobachten und sowohl aktuell als auch hintergründig darauf reagieren. Und wir geben Praktiker*innen und Forscher*innen eine Plattform.

**Gibt es einen Beitrag, Schwerpunkt oder Moment aus zehn Jahren Wissenschaftskommunikation.de, der Euch besonders in Erinnerung geblieben ist?**

Weißkopf: Es ist schwierig einen einzelnen Beitrag herauszuheben. Grundsätzlich finde ich es großartig, dass es gelungen ist, einen Ort für die Information über die Forschung zur Wissenschaftskommunikation zu schaffen. Das war mir, war uns, ein sehr wichtiges Anliegen: Die Evidenz aus der Forschung zu nutzen! Es kann nicht sein, dass ausgerechnet die Wissenschaftskommunikation sich nicht an den Erkenntnissen aus der Wissenschaft orientiert. Aber gerade das war in einem noch jungen Berufsfeld und ebenfalls recht jungen Forschungsfeld eine Herausforderung. Dass diese Forschung nun sichtbarer ist, ist sicher ein Verdienst von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de.

[Wo steht die Wisskomm? Alle Beiträge zum Schwerpunkt](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wo-steht-die-wisskomm/)

Leßmöllmann: Jedes Mal, wenn nach Monaten des Planens, Antragschreibens und Zitterns die Bewilligungsschreiben für die Weiterfinanzierung der Plattform kamen, haben Herausgeber*innen und Redaktion sehr gefeiert. Das waren besondere Momente: Nicht nur weitermachen zu können, sondern auch neue Ideen umzusetzen. Ein ganz besonderer Moment dauerte sogar eine ganze Woche: Der Designsprint mit der Deutschen Journalistenschule 2025, bei dem sich toller journalistische Nachwuchs in unser Portal reingekniet hat. Daraus ist unser großartiger [LinkedIn-Kanal](https://www.linkedin.com/company/wissenschaftskommunikation-de/) entstanden.

articleBody:
# Injured Ukrainian soldiers learn to use their new limbs | Psyche Videos

https://player.vimeo.com/video/1238020752

### Far from home, Ukrainian soldiers relearn to inhabit their bodies

It’s estimated that as many as 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers and civilians have lost a limb since Russia began its full-scale invasion in 2022. At the Protez Foundation in Oakdale, Minnesota, such patients are fitted with state-of-the-art prosthetics free of charge and are taught how to use their new limbs. However, as the stirring short documentary Liminal captures, the process is far more than just physical.

For the film, the director Brennan Vance profiled a group of Ukrainian soldiers who, injured on the front lines, came to Minnesota to recover far from the brutal war that had defined their lives for years. Yet, despite their life-altering injuries, most were still eager to continue fighting, especially as the US commitment to the cause seemed to be waning. With the encouraging guidance of Yakov Gradinar, the Ukrainian-American chief medical officer at the Protez Foundation, the young men learned not only how to be in their bodies once again, but also how to inhabit the world. Poignant and inspiring, Vance’s documentary is both a unique window into the ongoing conflict and a powerful portrait of what it means to suffer a profound loss and yet still find a way forward.

Director: Brennan Vance

Producers: Norah Shapiro, Brennan Vance

### The Best Fiction Books » Humour

## The Funniest Books of 2026

#### recommended by Sophie Ratcliffe

Every year, the judges of the Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for Comic Fiction select the funniest novel published in the past twelve months. In 2026, finalists include a Booker-nominated book about a man in a black bag and a Regency rom-com with a very modern sensibility. Judge, academic and author Sophie Ratcliffe talks us through the six-book shortlist.

Interview by Cal Flyn, Deputy Editor

Buy all books

- Read

### We Love You, Bunny: A Novel by Mona Awad

### 1A Good Person by Kirsten King

### 2Black Bag: A Novel by Luke Kennard

### 3How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin

### 4Motherfaker by Anna Brook-Mitchell

### 5Offseason by Avigayl Sharp

### 6We Love You, Bunny: A Novel by Mona Awad

Thank you for talking to us about the six-book shortlist for the 2026 Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for comic fiction. I wonder: is judging humorous writing unusually difficult?

Yes, I think there is a difficulty. I guess what different people find funny or ‘comic’ is pretty subjective. It sounds a touch grave to say that it feels like a responsibility, but it is. We were all trying to come to these books with as open a mind as possible about the varieties of humour that we might encounter. We, as a panel, were looking for books that would make us laugh out loud, but were were also open to those that made us smile or raise an eyebrow, which plunged us into the absurd and grotesque, or the dry and the wry…

Also, crucially, we wanted books that were exceptionally well-written. My own acid test for any really great book – particularly a great comic or joy-giving book – is that I want to press it into the hands of someone who, say, tells me they are going into hospital and need something good to read. Maybe that sounds vague, but these were the rough ingredients of the recipe we were looking for.

A funny book is not the same thing as a light read. They can be both, but a great funny book should still be a quality book.

That’s right. And when I look at the shortlist from this year, that comes through.

Let’s look at those books, one at a time. Can we start with A Good Person by Kirsten King? It features a modern-day hex.

I love this one. Here’s the plot. The heroine of this book breaks up with her boyfriend, who she spent quite a lot of time getting. She also works for a marketing company, and through her work encounters the ‘Wellness Witch’, a social influencer, who gives her the tools to put a ‘hex’ on her ex.

It’s very filmic – King is a screenwriter, and you can tell. I think what stands out in this one is the voice. It’s so good, full of very funny one-liners, which are integrated beautifully. It’s also a page-turner.

The title is A Good Person, and it is very thoughtful about ethics, carried with a light touch. It makes one think about what that means, to be a good person, and what it might be like to want to hex someone, and what to do with shame when things get out of control.

Then all of that is played through a sort of millennial angst about paying rent and having roommates. It’s a gorgeous piece of work: quite dark, very funny.

It’s a classic combination. Comedians are famously troubled. Is there a thread of darkness running through all of the books?

In many of them, yes. There’s quite a lot of trauma and darkness to negotiate in this list. But what the books have in common is that while the dark recesses of the soul might be pondered or traversed, the joke always lands at home. The thread these books have in common is that the comedy is entwined with kindness. They certainly don’t punch down.

Luke Kennard’s Black Bag also featured on the Booker Prize shortlist, which I was delighted to see. I think it’s great. Why did the Wodehouse Prize judges admire it?

Well, it made us all laugh out loud. That’s the first thing. I don’t know if that is the most important thing to say about it, but for this prize it is very important. It’s not a book that is safe to read on a train because you will spill your coffee. And, actually, there’s a fantastic scene involving a coffee mishap—

Yes!

It’s a really, really funny book. So the scenario is based on a real-life psychological experiment where a professor hired someone to wear a large, leather, full-body black bag around the campus of a university to see what happened. So that is clearly completely absurd. The person in this book who is performing as the black bag is a failed actor, and this ‘part’ becomes his starring role. We admired the huge comedy of the novel, but in its construction, Black Bag has really thought through this comic scenario and what it can tell us about what it means to make art, and what it is like to be a human being.

Again, this is a book that does not laugh at anyone, but rather at the predicament of what it means to be human. We also loved the physical comedy. The tiny details. The actor wearing the black bag immacs his lower legs to make sure that no one can work out whether he’s male or female. And he talks brilliantly to the visceral feeling of wearing hot, black leather. There are also interesting themes which emerge around another character who makes a living through livestreams and cryptocurrency. So this book makes us ponder the relationship between the virtual and the material.

It’s a very clever book, but with great humour. You’re physically wincing as you read. It’s masterly.

Well, we have a very different book up next. This is How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin. It’s a Regency rom-com. Tell us more.

One thing I want to highlight about this book is that it is gorgeously reflexive. It begins with the heroine reading a novel. The title too, is a riff on How to Lose a Guy in Ten Days, the Kate Hudson and Matthew McConaughey film.

Plotwise, it’s a Regency comedy in which both members of the couple are trying to break off an engagement, but modernity keeps poking its nose through the pages. You get a sense, almost, that they are wearing sneakerinas under their muslin frocks. It’s an enjoyable historical novel, but also a comedy about what it means to write historical fiction. It’s clever and quite delicious – probably the lightest book on the list.

I did want to give a shout out to some of the period descriptions: There’s a moment when Lydia takes a seat between a beef tremblant and a pigeon à la crapaudine. And there are descriptions of characters galloping ventre à terre, a Georgette Heyer term – if somebody really loves you, they will ride so that their horse’s belly is grazing the ground.

So, yes, romantic, but it’s a story not just about the characters but how we reimagine history. It laughs at, and with us, for wanting to revisit the past.

I love that. And the fondness that comes through for the genre itself, and the writers that came before. Mocking can be a kind of flattery. Shall we talk about Anna Brook-Mitchell’s Motherfaker? This novel has a great concept. I’ve heard of fake relationship novels, but fake pregnancy is a new one on me.

Well, if you want a how-to guide, I know now that in order to fake a pregnancy you need a variety of sizes of fake stomachs.

As soon as you say it, I think: Of course.

And you will probably need to bond with these different stomachs by giving them names when you wear them. That would help.

The main character is a teacher, who is becoming increasingly infuriated by the cult of the child in her workplace – the fact that her colleagues keep taking maternity leave or leaving her to do all the work while they attend baby yoga or sports days. Through a variety of circumstances, she ends up pretending to be pregnant. So, it’s a concept driven novel focussing on what happens when a scenario gets out of control. That’s quite intriguing, I guess, because in some ways being pregnant is rather out of one’s control.

Again, Brook-Mitchell is super good on physical comedy. And as you said, we often have plots involving people “passing” for different identity categories. But I’ve never encountered one about passing as pregnant.

But the book does have a core of sadness and anger to it. There is something both hilarious and deeply plangent about someone taping latex imaginary futures to themselves, about conjuring a baby.

It feels quite timely, with the rise of the child-free movement. By taking the idea to a comedic extreme, does it force us to some new thinking on the subject?

Yes. It connects with a great book by Sarah Knott, Mother Is A Verb. I think it does try to remind us – in a light way – that to mother is to nurture, and that this is open to everyone, not the domain of a particular few.

Thank you. Can we talk about the fifth book on the 2026 Wodehouse Prize shortlist? This is Offseason by Avigayl Sharp, a novel set in an all-girls boarding school. This was completely new to me.

So this is wild. Offseason is offbeat, off key. The narrator, heroine, is also a teacher. She’s been hired to cover teach for a term at a private school in a remote town on US coastal seaboard. It’s the off season there, so it’s quite empty, bleak and dark. But I guess the ‘off season’ also reminds us of the theatrical nature of what it means to be, or not to be, acting a role. And there’s a lot of comedy and tragedy in this novel about the roles and games people play. It’s also hugely focused on questions of negotiating trauma, and there’s a biting wit in relation to that.

She’s just dropped out of her PhD, our heroine-narrator, and there are there are some standout comic scenes about teaching. Like when she tries to correct a basic error made by a student, and her charge starts to ‘weep openly. Tears ran from the corner of her eyes down to her mouth, where her tongue flicked out automatically to lap them up’. Our narrator then furiously back-pedals, ‘I quickly tried to think of tender remarks that would make Anita stop crying so that I would not get fired and have to move back in with my parents’. The deadpan comic rhythm of that sentence, which moves from compassion to narcissism gives you a sense of this book.

And I also thought this was an interesting book, politically. It has two ghost texts underneath it: Bleak House – the class set text. And Sharp, like Dickens, is interested in who gets to be a main character and who doesn’t, in the people that cities ‘forget’. Meanwhile, it also has an epigraph from The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie. And there’s a lot, in this novel, as with Spark, about searching for a hero, for a story, for a meta-narrative, to find one’s way.

I’d say that the thing that makes this novel so particularly dark is that you spend all the time in our heroine’s mind. Actually, almost all of these books are in the first person in one way or another, but this is a mind that you’re quite glad to get out of.

She’s described as giving “manic” lectures.

Yes, you’re in the intensity of her thoughts, and those thoughts are, well, messy and full of snot and vomit and sex.

I think that might bring us to the final book on the shortlist, which is Mona Awad’s We Love You, Bunny. It’s described as ‘horror-satire’ which is an intriguing mash-up.

Yes. I’d say dark academia. Donna Tartt crossed with Alice in Wonderland, performed by the cast of Heathers.

I’m listening.

It’s about a group of obsessive MFA students who are holding hostage one of their former cohort. They are all telling their stories. The plot is centrally about storytelling, and in some ways you could see it as a sort of working-out of what Faulkner said about killing your darlings. (And these narrators are all, literally, darlings. They are all concerned with writing and floral prints and satin and nail polish, and they call each other ‘Bunny.’ ) Again, it’s very intense, completely absurd, magical realist.

They’re on a MFA course, and they are all comparing what the professor has fed back on what they have produced and performing their responses to it. One says:

How I cried and cried in the rose garden about his formatting comments. Actually totally inconsolable. How dare he suggest that I change the shape of my story? That I break up my paragraph further? It’s like he’s insisting I change the shape of me or something.

I did love this. Each of the narrators, as they are talking through what has happened, touches on the idea of the writing ego and the idea of inspiration. So I found this absurd and completely unexpected.

The MFA workshop format is ripe for a good comedy of manners.

Yes. And there are a lot of campus novels here on this list. Many of our list were, it seems, drawn to that sense of the closed world and its potential playing out big ethical questions of how we manage to be human and how we connect with other people. In Offseason we have the boarding school; in Motherfaker, she’s also a teacher.

Black Bag is set in a university. Then there’s this.

I was intrigued by that common thread. The campus with its potential for playing out ethical and imaginative questions. In We Love You, Bunny, it’s ego and creativity. In Black Bag, perhaps it’s big questions of how we connect with other people.

Right. In a closed community, you can allow the pressure to build until it becomes absurd. Otherwise, would you offer any other takeaways from the judging process? Did you find it easy or hard to come to a consensus?

There was a lot of consensus in what we were looking for. What I enjoyed about the group was that someone would say, oh, this is funny, and another person would be able to speak to the construction of it – something that explains why it is funny, which you had felt in your heart but hadn’t seen. That’s what I really enjoyed.

In some sense, I think the judging process was not so much one of resolving disagreement but of helping each other shed light on articulating why each book should be on the shortlist. All the books on there are brilliantly written and constructed, and independently we came to the same decisions – and together we were able to justify that.

I do feel these books are friends. They are not rivals, but compatriots. And so in some ways it will just be about deciding which best fits the bill for this prize. We’re a convivial bunch and I know we won’t leave the room until everyone is in total agreement.

Interview by Cal Flyn, Deputy Editor

## The Funniest Books of 2026

#### recommended by Sophie Ratcliffe

Every year, the judges of the Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for Comic Fiction select the funniest novel published in the past twelve months. In 2026, finalists include a Booker-nominated book about a man in a black bag and a Regency rom-com with a very modern sensibility. Judge, academic and author Sophie Ratcliffe talks us through the six-book shortlist.

Interview by Cal Flyn, Deputy Editor

### 1A Good Person by Kirsten King

### 2Black Bag: A Novel by Luke Kennard

### 3How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin

### 4Motherfaker by Anna Brook-Mitchell

### 5Offseason by Avigayl Sharp

### 6We Love You, Bunny: A Novel by Mona Awad

Thank you for talking to us about the six-book shortlist for the 2026 Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for comic fiction. I wonder: is judging humorous writing unusually difficult?

Yes, I think there is a difficulty. I guess what different people find funny or ‘comic’ is pretty subjective. It sounds a touch grave to say that it feels like a responsibility, but it is. We were all trying to come to these books with as open a mind as possible about the varieties of humour that we might encounter. We, as a panel, were looking for books that would make us laugh out loud, but were were also open to those that made us smile or raise an eyebrow, which plunged us into the absurd and grotesque, or the dry and the wry…

Also, crucially, we wanted books that were exceptionally well-written. My own acid test for any really great book – particularly a great comic or joy-giving book – is that I want to press it into the hands of someone who, say, tells me they are going into hospital and need something good to read. Maybe that sounds vague, but these were the rough ingredients of the recipe we were looking for.

A funny book is not the same thing as a light read. They can be both, but a great funny book should still be a quality book.

That’s right. And when I look at the shortlist from this year, that comes through.

Let’s look at those books, one at a time. Can we start with A Good Person by Kirsten King? It features a modern-day hex.

I love this one. Here’s the plot. The heroine of this book breaks up with her boyfriend, who she spent quite a lot of time getting. She also works for a marketing company, and through her work encounters the ‘Wellness Witch’, a social influencer, who gives her the tools to put a ‘hex’ on her ex.

It’s very filmic – King is a screenwriter, and you can tell. I think what stands out in this one is the voice. It’s so good, full of very funny one-liners, which are integrated beautifully. It’s also a page-turner.

The title is A Good Person, and it is very thoughtful about ethics, carried with a light touch. It makes one think about what that means, to be a good person, and what it might be like to want to hex someone, and what to do with shame when things get out of control.

Then all of that is played through a sort of millennial angst about paying rent and having roommates. It’s a gorgeous piece of work: quite dark, very funny.

It’s a classic combination. Comedians are famously troubled. Is there a thread of darkness running through all of the books?

In many of them, yes. There’s quite a lot of trauma and darkness to negotiate in this list. But what the books have in common is that while the dark recesses of the soul might be pondered or traversed, the joke always lands at home. The thread these books have in common is that the comedy is entwined with kindness. They certainly don’t punch down.

Luke Kennard’s Black Bag also featured on the Booker Prize shortlist, which I was delighted to see. I think it’s great. Why did the Wodehouse Prize judges admire it?

Well, it made us all laugh out loud. That’s the first thing. I don’t know if that is the most important thing to say about it, but for this prize it is very important. It’s not a book that is safe to read on a train because you will spill your coffee. And, actually, there’s a fantastic scene involving a coffee mishap—

Yes!

It’s a really, really funny book. So the scenario is based on a real-life psychological experiment where a professor hired someone to wear a large, leather, full-body black bag around the campus of a university to see what happened. So that is clearly completely absurd. The person in this book who is performing as the black bag is a failed actor, and this ‘part’ becomes his starring role. We admired the huge comedy of the novel, but in its construction, Black Bag has really thought through this comic scenario and what it can tell us about what it means to make art, and what it is like to be a human being.

Again, this is a book that does not laugh at anyone, but rather at the predicament of what it means to be human. We also loved the physical comedy. The tiny details. The actor wearing the black bag immacs his lower legs to make sure that no one can work out whether he’s male or female. And he talks brilliantly to the visceral feeling of wearing hot, black leather. There are also interesting themes which emerge around another character who makes a living through livestreams and cryptocurrency. So this book makes us ponder the relationship between the virtual and the material.

It’s a very clever book, but with great humour. You’re physically wincing as you read. It’s masterly.

Well, we have a very different book up next. This is How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin. It’s a Regency rom-com. Tell us more.

One thing I want to highlight about this book is that it is gorgeously reflexive. It begins with the heroine reading a novel. The title too, is a riff on How to Lose a Guy in Ten Days, the Kate Hudson and Matthew McConaughey film.

Plotwise, it’s a Regency comedy in which both members of the couple are trying to break off an engagement, but modernity keeps poking its nose through the pages. You get a sense, almost, that they are wearing sneakerinas under their muslin frocks. It’s an enjoyable historical novel, but also a comedy about what it means to write historical fiction. It’s clever and quite delicious – probably the lightest book on the list.

I did want to give a shout out to some of the period descriptions: There’s a moment when Lydia takes a seat between a beef tremblant and a pigeon à la crapaudine. And there are descriptions of characters galloping ventre à terre, a Georgette Heyer term – if somebody really loves you, they will ride so that their horse’s belly is grazing the ground.

So, yes, romantic, but it’s a story not just about the characters but how we reimagine history. It laughs at, and with us, for wanting to revisit the past.

I love that. And the fondness that comes through for the genre itself, and the writers that came before. Mocking can be a kind of flattery. Shall we talk about Anna Brook-Mitchell’s Motherfaker? This novel has a great concept. I’ve heard of fake relationship novels, but fake pregnancy is a new one on me.

Well, if you want a how-to guide, I know now that in order to fake a pregnancy you need a variety of sizes of fake stomachs.

As soon as you say it, I think: Of course.

And you will probably need to bond with these different stomachs by giving them names when you wear them. That would help.

The main character is a teacher, who is becoming increasingly infuriated by the cult of the child in her workplace – the fact that her colleagues keep taking maternity leave or leaving her to do all the work while they attend baby yoga or sports days. Through a variety of circumstances, she ends up pretending to be pregnant. So, it’s a concept driven novel focussing on what happens when a scenario gets out of control. That’s quite intriguing, I guess, because in some ways being pregnant is rather out of one’s control.

Again, Brook-Mitchell is super good on physical comedy. And as you said, we often have plots involving people “passing” for different identity categories. But I’ve never encountered one about passing as pregnant.

But the book does have a core of sadness and anger to it. There is something both hilarious and deeply plangent about someone taping latex imaginary futures to themselves, about conjuring a baby.

It feels quite timely, with the rise of the child-free movement. By taking the idea to a comedic extreme, does it force us to some new thinking on the subject?

Yes. It connects with a great book by Sarah Knott, Mother Is A Verb. I think it does try to remind us – in a light way – that to mother is to nurture, and that this is open to everyone, not the domain of a particular few.

Thank you. Can we talk about the fifth book on the 2026 Wodehouse Prize shortlist? This is Offseason by Avigayl Sharp, a novel set in an all-girls boarding school. This was completely new to me.

So this is wild. Offseason is offbeat, off key. The narrator, heroine, is also a teacher. She’s been hired to cover teach for a term at a private school in a remote town on US coastal seaboard. It’s the off season there, so it’s quite empty, bleak and dark. But I guess the ‘off season’ also reminds us of the theatrical nature of what it means to be, or not to be, acting a role. And there’s a lot of comedy and tragedy in this novel about the roles and games people play. It’s also hugely focused on questions of negotiating trauma, and there’s a biting wit in relation to that.

She’s just dropped out of her PhD, our heroine-narrator, and there are there are some standout comic scenes about teaching. Like when she tries to correct a basic error made by a student, and her charge starts to ‘weep openly. Tears ran from the corner of her eyes down to her mouth, where her tongue flicked out automatically to lap them up’. Our narrator then furiously back-pedals, ‘I quickly tried to think of tender remarks that would make Anita stop crying so that I would not get fired and have to move back in with my parents’. The deadpan comic rhythm of that sentence, which moves from compassion to narcissism gives you a sense of this book.

And I also thought this was an interesting book, politically. It has two ghost texts underneath it: Bleak House – the class set text. And Sharp, like Dickens, is interested in who gets to be a main character and who doesn’t, in the people that cities ‘forget’. Meanwhile, it also has an epigraph from The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie. And there’s a lot, in this novel, as with Spark, about searching for a hero, for a story, for a meta-narrative, to find one’s way.

I’d say that the thing that makes this novel so particularly dark is that you spend all the time in our heroine’s mind. Actually, almost all of these books are in the first person in one way or another, but this is a mind that you’re quite glad to get out of.

She’s described as giving “manic” lectures.

Yes, you’re in the intensity of her thoughts, and those thoughts are, well, messy and full of snot and vomit and sex.

I think that might bring us to the final book on the shortlist, which is Mona Awad’s We Love You, Bunny. It’s described as ‘horror-satire’ which is an intriguing mash-up.

Yes. I’d say dark academia. Donna Tartt crossed with Alice in Wonderland, performed by the cast of Heathers.

I’m listening.

It’s about a group of obsessive MFA students who are holding hostage one of their former cohort. They are all telling their stories. The plot is centrally about storytelling, and in some ways you could see it as a sort of working-out of what Faulkner said about killing your darlings. (And these narrators are all, literally, darlings. They are all concerned with writing and floral prints and satin and nail polish, and they call each other ‘Bunny.’ ) Again, it’s very intense, completely absurd, magical realist.

They’re on a MFA course, and they are all comparing what the professor has fed back on what they have produced and performing their responses to it. One says:

How I cried and cried in the rose garden about his formatting comments. Actually totally inconsolable. How dare he suggest that I change the shape of my story? That I break up my paragraph further? It’s like he’s insisting I change the shape of me or something.

I did love this. Each of the narrators, as they are talking through what has happened, touches on the idea of the writing ego and the idea of inspiration. So I found this absurd and completely unexpected.

The MFA workshop format is ripe for a good comedy of manners.

Yes. And there are a lot of campus novels here on this list. Many of our list were, it seems, drawn to that sense of the closed world and its potential playing out big ethical questions of how we manage to be human and how we connect with other people. In Offseason we have the boarding school; in Motherfaker, she’s also a teacher.

Black Bag is set in a university. Then there’s this.

I was intrigued by that common thread. The campus with its potential for playing out ethical and imaginative questions. In We Love You, Bunny, it’s ego and creativity. In Black Bag, perhaps it’s big questions of how we connect with other people.

Right. In a closed community, you can allow the pressure to build until it becomes absurd. Otherwise, would you offer any other takeaways from the judging process? Did you find it easy or hard to come to a consensus?

There was a lot of consensus in what we were looking for. What I enjoyed about the group was that someone would say, oh, this is funny, and another person would be able to speak to the construction of it – something that explains why it is funny, which you had felt in your heart but hadn’t seen. That’s what I really enjoyed.

In some sense, I think the judging process was not so much one of resolving disagreement but of helping each other shed light on articulating why each book should be on the shortlist. All the books on there are brilliantly written and constructed, and independently we came to the same decisions – and together we were able to justify that.

I do feel these books are friends. They are not rivals, but compatriots. And so in some ways it will just be about deciding which best fits the bill for this prize. We’re a convivial bunch and I know we won’t leave the room until everyone is in total agreement.
