articleBody:
Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly [Opportunities Newsletter](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/newsletter/opportunities/).

**[Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + Photo](https://innovateartistgrants.org)** **Featured**
Innovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. Nine honorable mentions in each category are also featured on the Innovate Grant platform and join a growing creative community of esteemed artists. Applicants must be 18 years and older, and all media and genres are accepted. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 15, 2026.**

**[Bryson County Retreat](https://www.brysoncountyretreat.org/)** **Featured**
Practicing artists of any background and at any stage of their career are encouraged to apply for a 2027 residency at Bryson County Retreat. Residency periods can be flexible, but month-long stays are suggested. Bryson County is designed to provide ample living and working space and inspirational settings where an artist may work free from the distractions and responsibilities of day-to-day life. The program includes free lodging near tannic dark water lakes, sprawling live oaks, and drooping Spanish moss at the headwaters of the Santa Fe River in north central Florida.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**Open Calls**

**[Wildlife Photographer of the Year](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/wildlife-photographer-of-the-year/competition.html)** *(International)*
Alongside its conservation message, this prestigious global competition is hosted by London’s Natural History Museum to champion the work of photographers, whether professional or amateur, young or older, or using top-of-the-range equipment or smartphones. Photographers are eligible for myriad awards, with a Grand Title prize of £15,000. The entry fee is £35 (free for Young WPY contest).
**Deadline: 11:30 p.m. GMT on December 3, 2026.**

**[Responsa Foundation Open Call for Textile Art](https://responsafoundation.com/2026/10/13/this-memory-competition/)** *(International)*
The Responsa Foundation champions projects that create meaningful social impact and foster public engagement. The organization is seeking textile artists to submit work for *This Memory,* a group exhibition taking place from September 22 to October 3, 2027, at Burgh House in Hampstead.
**Deadline: December 4, 2026.**

**[Open Call for Public Art Proposals in Moab](https://www.moabarts.org/public-art-application)** (Utah, National)
Moab Arts is accepting proposals for 2027 public art projects. Proposals are welcome for sculpture, murals, three crosswalks, and sticker designs but may include other ideas for different media or locations around the city. Preference is given to local and regional artists.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MST on December 6, 2026.**

**[Material Works Art Award 2026](https://pci.jotform.com/form/262185636090156)** *(International)*
Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.
**Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.**

**[Call for Mail Art](https://www.hivebookarts.org/exhibitions/call-for-mail-art)** *(International)*
Hive Center for the Book Arts in Evanston, Illinois, welcomes mail art for the exhibition *love|mark*, which runs from January 1 to February 27. All submissions must arrive at at the center by December 15 for inclusion in the show.
**Deadline:** **December 15, 2026.**

**[Sony Future Filmmaker Awards](https://www.sonyfuturefilmmakerawards.com/)** *(International)*
The Sony Future Filmmaker Awards is a major program providing opportunities for creators and filmmakers. The shortlisted filmmakers are flown to Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City, California, to attend an awards ceremony and an industry immersion program. Categories include fiction, nonfiction, animation, immersive, student, and vertical format.
**Deadline: 7 a.m. CST on December 15, 2026.**

**[GLEAM 2027 Request for Proposals](https://www.olbrichgleam.org/submit-a-proposal)** *(International)*
Olbrich Botanical Gardens in Madison, Wisconsin, invites proposals for temporary, large-scale, light-based artwork for *GLEAM*, a public art exhibition. The show will be open to the public from August 28 to October 23, 2027.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. CST on January 6, 2027.**

**[Visual Arts Prize IDEA – Vila d’Amer](https://www.ideagc.com/en/idea-mundoarti/)** *(International)*
Apply for this inaugural prize open to artists working in all visual arts media. Two winning artworks, with prizes of €3,500 and €1,500, will become part of the permanent International Visual Arts Collection IDEA – Vila d’Amer.
**Deadline: January 10, 2027.**

**[360 CHICAGO: CloudWalk Call for Artists](https://360chicago.com/cloudwalk-call-for-artists)** *(Chicago)*
One artist will be selected for this major installation in the CloudWalk gallery atop 875 N. Michigan Ave. The selected artist receives a $10,000 commission, and the winning installation will go on view starting April 2027.
**Deadline: January 18, 2027.**

**[World of WearableArt 2027 Competition](https://www.worldofwearableart.com/competition/entry-information)** *(International)*
Entries are now open for the 2027 WOW Competition in Wellington, New Zealand. Awards consist of NZ$200,000 in prizes, including the Supreme WOW Award of NZ$30,000.
**Deadline: February 11, 2027 (international), March 31, 2027 (New Zealand).**

**Grants**

**[The Filmed in Nevada County Grant](https://nevadacityfilmfestival.com/filmedinnc/)** *(International)*
To support filmmakers in the production of work in Nevada County, California, Nevada City Film Festival offers grants between $1,000 and $20,000.
**Deadline: December 1, 2026.**

**[Southern Prize and State Fellowships for Visual Arts](https://www.southarts.org/grants-opportunities/southern-prize-and-state-fellowships-visual-arts)** *(U.S. South)*
The South Arts Southern Prize and State Fellowships acknowledge the highest quality artistic work being created in the American South. The program is open to individual artists living in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee. State Fellowships are $5,000, with one awarded per state. These then compete for two Southern Prize tiers of $25,000 and $10,000.
**Deadline: January 15, 2027 (fee waiver request by December 18, 2026).**

**[The Virigina A. Groot Foundation Grants](https://www.virginiaagrootfoundation.org/grants/)** *(International)*
Each year, the Virginia A. Groot Foundation offers three grants to artists who have exceptional talent and a demonstrated ability in ceramic sculpture or sculpture of diverse mediums. The grants are organized into tiers, with the top award providing $60,000, the second award offering $30,000, and the third awarding $20,000.
**Deadline: January 9, 2027.**

**[Foundation for Contemporary Arts](https://www.foundationforcontemporaryarts.org/grants/emergency-grants/)** **[Emergency Grants](https://www.foundationforcontemporaryarts.org/grants/emergency-grants/)** *(U.S.)*
Emergency Grants provide urgent funding for visual and performing artists and poets who have sudden, unanticipated opportunities to present their work to the public, but there is insufficient time to seek other sources of funding or unexpected expenses are incurred for projects close to completion. Each month, the organization makes approximately 15 to 20 grants in the range of $500 to $3,000 each.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**[National Lottery Project Grants](https://www.artscouncil.org.uk/ProjectGrants/national-lottery-project-grants-guidance-library)** *(U.K.)*
Both individuals and organizations can apply to Arts Council National Lottery Project Grants. These awards are designed to focus on specific projects with starting and ending dates including festivals and carnivals, dance, libraries, literature, museums, music, theater, or visual arts programs. There is no maximum threshold for the fund.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**[Black Artists Grant](https://commonwealthfoundation.com/opportunity/black-artists-grant/)** *(U.K.)*
The Black Artists Grant offered by Creative Debuts is no-strings-attached financial support to help Black artists. Selected applicants receive £500, and applications are reviewed monthly.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**[The Adolf and Esther Gottlieb Emergency Grant](https://www.gottliebfoundation.org/emergency-grant)** *(International)*
This program provides one-time financial assistance to qualified painters, printmakers, and sculptors whose needs resulted from an unforeseen catastrophic incident and who lack the resources to meet that situation. Awardees typically receive $5,000 and up to $15,000.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

[Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant](https://pkf.org/apply/) * (International)*
The foundation welcomes applications from painters, sculptors, and artists working on paper, including printmakers. Grants are intended for one year and range up to $50,000. The artist’s circumstances determine the size of the grant, and professional exhibition history will be considered.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**Residencies, Fellowships, & More**

**[Kent Cultural Alliance Spring 2027 SERVICE Residency](https://kentculture.org/residency/)** *(U.S.)*
Artists are invited to apply for a six-week residency session in Chestertown, Maryland, devoted to the theme of service. Each selected artist will receive a $7,500 stipend for the six-week session, a travel reimbursement up to $1,000, and studio and gallery expense reimbursement up to $1,500.
**Deadline: 5 p.m. EST on December 1, 2026.**

**[Charles Allis Art Museum Artist in Residence](https://www.charlesallis.org/learn_about/artist_in_residence_/)** *(International)*
Located in Milwaukee’s Lower East Side neighborhood, the Charles Allis Art Museum residency program gives one artist the opportunity to engage with the Allis’ collection of more than 800 historic pieces from the early 20th century. The participant receives an $1,800 honorarium and up to a $400 travel stipend.
**Deadline: December 4, 2026.**

**[2026 McKnight Fellowships for Fiber Artists](https://textilecentermn.org/event/applications-open-for-2026-mcknight-fellowships-for-fiber-artists/)** *(Minnesota)*
Each year, the Textile Center awards two unrestricted $25,000 fellowships to post-emerging Minnesota fiber artists who demonstrate exceptional proficiency, sustained practice, and commitment to the field. Fellowship dates are March 1, 2027, to February 28, 2028.
**Deadline: December 7, 2026.**

**[Open AIR Residencies](https://www.openairmt.org/opportunities)** *(International)*
Open AIR is a Missoula-based nonprofit that brings artists and communities together through place-based residencies and public arts programs across Montana. Sessions currently accepting applications include summer 2027, fall 2027, and spring 2028.
**Deadline: December 7, 2026.**

**[Cove Park Awarded Residencies for 2027-28](https://covepark.org/awarded-residencies-2027-2028/)** *(International)*
Located in beautiful Argyll & Bute, Scotland, Cove Park awards funded residencies, in addition to travel, visa, materials, and access allowances when required. (Self-funded Open Residencies and subsidized winter residencies are open on [a rolling basis](https://covepark.org/current/).)
**Deadline: December 11, 2026.**

**[An Talla Solais Càirdeas/The Kinship Residency](https://www.antallasolais.org/opencall)** *(International)*
BIPOC artists working in any medium are invited to apply to this fully funded residency in Ullapool in the Scottish Highlands. The program runs throughout January, February, and March 2027. The residency covers all work space, housing, mentoring, and exhibition costs in addition to a £750 weekly stipend.
**Deadline: December 14, 2026.**

**[Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency 2027-28](https://www.jthar.org/)** *(International)*
Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency offers time and space amidst the natural beauty of Joshua Tree National Park. Seven-week residencies include scholarship funds, housing, and studio space designed to accommodate a broad range of artistic activity and open studio events. There is a $45 application fee.
**Deadline: December 15, 2026.**

**[ren AiR](https://www.ren.global/air)** *(International)*
ren is a discovery platform where you share everything that goes into your artistic practice. For its residency, four selected artists will each receive $5,000 to develop and realize a project of their choice, wherever they are based, while sharing their creative journey with the ren community. In addition, eight artists will receive $2,000 prizes.
**Deadline: December 31, 2026.**

# All our models of how the mind functions are missing something

## The energy of thought

### We have an astonishing number of models of how the mind works. All of them neglect something essential

The Moment the Snow Melts (2025), an installation by the Japanese artist Chiharu Shiota, in Milan, Italy. Photo by Emanuele Cremaschi/Getty Images

Listen to this essay

20 minutelisten

Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Some liken the mind to a computer. Some emphasise symbols and ‘mentalese’, a hypothesised ‘language of thought’. Some start from the brain and its physical, neural basis. These models aren’t necessarily in conflict: for instance, the ‘working memory’ model proposed by the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch may complement ‘predictive processing’ models of vision or attention theorised by the computational neuroscientists Rajesh Rao, Dana Ballard and Karl Friston. The domain is crowded, and still growing.

However, nearly all of these models neglect something essential to how the human mind functions: metabolism. They describe what the mind computes, or how its neurons signal, but not the metabolic work by which the brain acquires energy, maintains homeostasis, and disposes of waste. Without taking metabolism into consideration, our models are in danger of becoming untethered from real-world constraints, turning the ancient goal of understanding the mind into a wild goose chase.

So what happens if we take brain metabolism seriously?

‘Metabolism’ refers to activities that all biological systems, the brain included, carry out in order to stay alive. It includes energy use, but also maintenance, regulation and waste removal. Metabolism informs models of how our muscles work when we run, how our lungs work when we breathe, and how our immune system works when we get sick. Since the human mind has something to do with the brain, it stands to reason that metabolism should inform models of how our brain works when we think. And, indeed, most scholars nowadays tend to accept that the brain is important to understanding the mind, even if they leave it out of their models.

The brain is a quirky organ, metabolically speaking. It consumes a lot of energy compared with other parts of the human body. Though it makes up around 2 per cent of an adult’s body mass, it consumes about 20 per cent of its calories. Yet it is impressively efficient. The brain on average operates at about 20 watts – less than an incandescent lightbulb. A ‘lightbulb moment’, in other words, probably consumes less energy than an actual lightbulb.

According to one study by William Levy and Victoria Calvert of the University of Virginia, the electrical signals (or ‘spikes’) that send information use only about 3.5 watts. Building and strengthening synapses, which is how information is stored, uses about 1.3 watts. It is not entirely understood how the brain can do so much with so little, but part of the answer is evolution: organisms with more efficient brains had a selective advantage for searching for food and avoiding predators. The human mind operates under tremendous metabolic constraints.

A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support

Focusing on metabolism might seem to fly in the face of much philosophical analysis of the mind. Many philosophers set the brain aside when building their theories, freeing the mind from its substratum. One reason is the widespread acceptance of multiple realisability, a view first set out by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in the 1960s, which holds that the same mental states can be realised by different neural states. What determines a mental state is what it does, not what it’s made of. This is how an octopus could still feel pain, even if its brain is unlike ours – it’s the state that matters, not the physical substratum. Some philosophers go further, adopting John Haugeland’s notion of ‘medium independence’: if mental states are computations – a mainstream view in cognitive science – then these states are independent of the specific medium in which they are embodied. Mental states are defined by formal rules, and these same rules can be implemented in different media. The familiar analogy is the computer: the same software (the mind) can be run on different hardware (the brain). Both views reject the idea that there is a one-to-one match between the mind and the brain. They suggest that the mind can be fruitfully studied on its own terms, making metabolism irrelevant to modelling.

Yet even brain-friendly philosophers have largely disregarded brain metabolism. Patricia Churchland, who urged philosophers to learn neuroscience, co-wrote a 1988 paper that defined the aim of computational neuroscience as explaining how the brain’s signals are used ‘to represent and process information’. But the chemistry that maintains those signals was lost in this framing. The philosopher Carl Craver and colleagues stay close to the biological ground when they argue that mechanisms are ‘entities and activities organised such that they are productive of regular changes’, for example neurotransmitters binding to receptors. But here too the energy that makes those activities possible figures as a background condition rather than as part of the explanation.

We argue that metabolism constrains which models of the mind are viable. But that does not require the mind to be uniquely realised by the brain: metabolic constraints narrow the options without settling on a single one. Consider the example of memory storage. It could occur via different brain processes, or in nonbiological media like silicon-based digital computers. Whatever the medium, all these systems will be constrained by energy use, maintenance and waste removal. A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support, and studying metabolism is how we find out where that limit lies.

So the metabolic constraints on physical systems like brains cannot be ignored when modelling the mind. This means rethinking our stance towards views like multiple realisability and medium independence. Rather than taking them to be firm metaphysical commitments, we should think of them as working hypotheses: great starting points, but open to revision after new research.

Recently, the philosophers Mazviita Chirimuuta, Corey Maley and Rosa Cao have each argued that information-processing in brains depends on signal amplitudes, metabolic molecules and energy supply. This suggests a tight link between mind and metabolism, but it does not decisively rule out multiple realisability or medium independence. Instead, it shows that studying brain metabolism can test how much these hypotheses help us understand the mind. Looking at metabolism is therefore important, even if future science finds out that there is no one-to-one relation between mind and brain, that minds can exist in silicon, or that body and environment are essential for cognition.

Molecules that make up a synapse are replaced within days, yet some memories last a lifetime

The past 25 years have seen great advances in our understanding of brain metabolism, providing us with a wealth of material for studying metabolic constraints on the mind. We now have detailed energy budgets: the brain devotes about 16 per cent of its energy to generating action potentials, 44 per cent to transmitting these signals chemically at the synapse, and 40 per cent to maintaining and repairing neuron cells. This means that only 60 per cent of brain energy is for signalling, while the rest is spent keeping the neural machinery from falling apart. According to a 2015 paper by the neuroscientists Elisabeth Engl and David Attwell, energy for maintenance and repair ‘must contribute to limiting the cognitive abilities of the brain because the total energy use of the brain constrains the temporal rate at which information can be encoded and processed.’ But budgets like this are too coarse on their own to serve as constraints, especially when modelling individual cognitive capacities. Numerical costs of information-processing, by contrast, are more specific. According to one study by the theoretical neuroscientist Jan Karbowski and colleagues, storing one bit of information in the synapse costs about 500,000 ATP (the ‘fuel’ of the cell).

Return to the example of memory. How can metabolism help us assess whether a model of memory is plausible? The dominant theoretical framework in neuroscience is that memory is stored in synapses: the junctions where signals pass from one neuron another. When a new memory is formed, the synapses change, affecting the signals that are transmitted. One such change is known as ‘Hebbian learning’, named for the neuropsychologist Donald Hebb, whose work is summed up in the slogan (not his) ‘neurons that fire together, wire together’.

Models are useful when they solve a theory’s problems, and the synaptic theory has two big ones. The first, often called interference, is that synapses that change easily are good at storing new memories but bad at keeping old ones. Almost any change in neural firing alters a synapse’s molecular makeup slightly. But then how do new memories keep from overwriting old ones? The second problem is called turnover. Molecules that make up a synapse are replaced within days, yet some memories last a lifetime. In order to stay alive, neurons must constantly rebuild their decaying parts. A neuron is like Otto Neurath’s ship, rebuilt plank by plank at sea. How does information survive in a system whose every part is being replaced?

In 2016, Stefano Fusi and Marcus Benna published a mathematical model to solve the interference problem. It asks us to imagine the synaptic memory process as a set of beakers – each standing for a chemical process at the synapse – filled with liquid and connected by tubes. The level in the first beaker is the synapse’s strength: adding liquid strengthens it, and removing liquid weakens it. ‘Over time,’ Benna explained in an interview, ‘the resulting flow of liquid will diffuse across the other beakers, corresponding to the long-term storage of memories.’ Because those deeper beakers fill and drain more slowly, they hold a trace of past changes and keep drawing the first beaker back towards its old level. New memories form quickly; old ones fade only slowly, as the levels even out.

However, metabolic constraints render this solution implausible. The beaker model describes a system in which biochemical processes in the synapse even out over time: liquid can flow one way or the other, but it ultimately reaches equilibrium. In biology, settling into equilibrium means death. As the physicist Erwin Schrödinger put it: ‘Living matter evades the decay to equilibrium.’ Neurons must take in and expel ions and molecules to stay alive. A neuron that reaches equilibrium loses its organisation and can no longer perform functions such as storing memories at the synapse. Treating metabolism as a constraint shows us that a linear beaker model does not solve the problem of forming new synaptic memories and keeping old ones. This consequence is easy to miss if modellers do not consider the relevance of metabolism.

Metabolism itself, though, points to a better model. Karbowski has developed a model of synaptic memory in which metabolism takes centre stage. Because living systems are never at equilibrium, he builds his model with the mathematics of nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Unlike the beaker model, this framework describes the resting state of the synapse as not being in equilibrium with its environment, and thus capable of storing memories.

Holding on to old memories costs so little that the synapse can afford to keep them while laying down new ones

The model links biochemical processes at the synapse in cycles rather than in linear sequences (as in the beaker model). ATP powers transitions between states in the cycle, so metabolism is built into the model directly. These transitions represent how the synapse strengthens or weakens to store or erase memories. Because the state changes in the cycle have different rates, they never reach equilibrium. The synapse can form new memories and keep them over time without dying.

Karbowski then combines the cyclic model with the numerical costs of information-processing (such as the ATP cost per bit of memory storage). His calculations show that encoding new memories is energetically cheap, and so is, under certain conditions, storing them for a long time. That may explain why interference doesn’t erase long-lasting memories: holding on to them costs so little that the synapse can afford to keep old memories while laying down new ones. The same picture suggests an answer to the turnover problem: if a memory is held in a state that the synapse actively maintains, rather than in any particular molecules, it can outlast the molecules themselves, much as Neurath’s ship stays afloat precisely because it is constantly being rebuilt.

A second example of how metabolism can inform models comes from research on mental effort. When you start work in the morning, you feel fresh. But as the day grinds on and you’re writing your 700th email and attending your fifth meeting, tasks that were easy become gruelling. This is the cost of mental effort. How can mental effort be modelled? One possibility is the ego depletion model, developed by the psychologist Roy Baumeister and colleagues. It posits that performing effortful tasks depends on a finite resource: glucose in the brain. The decrease in performance is explained by the decrease of the resource.

But the model has been challenged on empirical grounds, such as difficulties with replicating its findings. As a result, researchers such as Robert Kurzban and colleagues have turned towards computational models of mental effort, in which the brain calculates the benefits and costs of staying on task versus switching to another activity. Proponents conclude that computational models are superior, and that metabolism is not relevant to model mental effort.

Yet the opposition between resource models such as ego depletion and computational models of mental effort is false. Ego depletion was undone partly by metabolic evidence: the brain’s glucose use barely changes during demanding tasks, far too little for an afternoon of self-control to run it down. That is metabolism doing just what we have described, ruling out a model the brain could not run. And computational models face metabolic questions of their own, because weighing the costs and benefits of staying on task is itself work that must be paid for. Neuroscientists such as Amitai Shenhav, Matthew Botvinick and Clay Holroyd believe this computational process takes place in a brain area known as the anterior cingulate cortex. We can use evidence about available energy to assess whether models of this process are feasible.

Some researchers already integrate metabolism into their models of mental effort. Alexandre Zénon and colleagues, for instance, posit that effortful tasks require the brain to process more information and therefore use slightly more energy. Since its energy budget has a hard upper limit, the brain needs to spend less energy on other tasks. Zénon and his team explicitly link metabolism to our subjective feeling of effort, which might reflect how fast metabolic changes build up during demanding tasks. Fatigue, in turn, might reflect our expectation that these changes will continue.

Likewise, Holroyd’s ‘controllosphere’ model starts from the theory of how the brain controls behaviour and draws on empirical findings that sustained mental effort produces waste in neurons. On this model, the feeling of effort is a signal to the brain to stop tasks that require high control, so that waste can be cleared before causing damage. Research on mental effort shows that including metabolism into models of the mind is not a mere theoretical possibility. It is already a practical reality.

Attention to metabolism and energy use can improve more than just our knowledge of biological organisms. It can also help our understanding of artificial neural networks at the heart of dramatic advances in artificial intelligence. While the speed of development is new, the link between AI and the brain is old, going back to the first neural network model in 1943, from pioneers such as Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, or ‘the perceptron’ of Frank Rosenblatt in 1958. Recent advances like LLMs (large language models) reignited existential questions about whether AI is really intelligent, or even conscious. Metabolism and energy use should inform how we approach these questions.

The relationship between AI and energy use is largely uncharted territory, and a metabolically informed perspective suggests where to start looking. Hyperscale data centres use a lot of energy, far beyond the 20 watts the human brain runs on. Yet in philosophy and cognitive science, views like medium independence lead scholars to think of AI in abstract, formal terms: while the physical basis of an AI system may vary, the computation, so the thought goes, is the same. This focus on abstract computation leads philosophers such as Luke Kersten and Leonard Dung to argue that AI systems could, in principle, duplicate human minds. But, in brains, energy constraints help determine which computations are performed in the first place. If the same holds for artificial systems, then whether a chip and a brain are running ‘the same’ computation cannot simply be assumed. It has to be found out.

Unlike brains, AI systems are things we design, so we can change how they use energy and see what follows

Our research belongs to a growing discussion of energy use and its role in modelling both brains and AI systems. For example, Cao and the neuroscientist Daniel Yamins have studied how AI models implement a highly abstract version of the mechanism that brains use to respond to novel visual stimuli. Cao and Yamins recognise that brains and engineered AI face different energy constraints, yet they consider energetics only abstractly, in terms of efficiency and optimisation. We propose instead to rethink energy use in AI from the bottom up. How an AI system uses energy is a modelling problem, which depends on scale, training data and details of grid infrastructure, just as the brain’s energy use depends on the details of its metabolism. This crucial parallel between studying brains and AI systems is missed when we focus on task optimisation alone. Modelling AI energy use informs how and when energetic differences lead to computational, perhaps even cognitive, differences.

Unlike brains, AI systems are things we design, so we can change how they use energy and see what follows. AI energy use is a practical problem that the study of metabolism can help tackle. Cognitive scientists such as Megan Peters are already looking to the brain to improve energy efficiency in AI. These projects highlight the practical benefits that come from studying brain metabolism for engineering projects like AI model building. They also have theoretical benefits: projects that include energy use serve as tests of philosophical positions like medium independence.

When it comes to figuring out how to model minds, it is time that researchers take a ‘metabolic turn’, to quote our colleague Patrick McGivern. Taking seriously how systems use energy and regulate themselves gives us new ways of addressing the toughest questions that we face in making sense of the mind.

Metabolism itself, though, points to a better model. Karbowski has developed a model of synaptic memory in which metabolism takes centre stage. Because living systems are never at equilibrium, he builds his model with the mathematics of nonequilibrium thermodynamics. It posits that performing effortful tasks depends on a finite resource: glucose in the brain. The decrease in performance is explained by the decrease of the resource.

# All our models of how the mind functions are missing something

## The energy of thought

### We have an astonishing number of models of how the mind works. All of them neglect something essential

The Moment the Snow Melts (2025), an installation by the Japanese artist Chiharu Shiota, in Milan, Italy. Photo by Emanuele Cremaschi/Getty Images

Listen to this essay

20 minutelisten

Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Some liken the mind to a computer. Some emphasise symbols and ‘mentalese’, a hypothesised ‘language of thought’. Some start from the brain and its physical, neural basis. These models aren’t necessarily in conflict: for instance, the ‘working memory’ model proposed by the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch may complement ‘predictive processing’ models of vision or attention theorised by the computational neuroscientists Rajesh Rao, Dana Ballard and Karl Friston. The domain is crowded, and still growing.

However, nearly all of these models neglect something essential to how the human mind functions: metabolism. They describe what the mind computes, or how its neurons signal, but not the metabolic work by which the brain acquires energy, maintains homeostasis, and disposes of waste. Without taking metabolism into consideration, our models are in danger of becoming untethered from real-world constraints, turning the ancient goal of understanding the mind into a wild goose chase.

So what happens if we take brain metabolism seriously?

‘Metabolism’ refers to activities that all biological systems, the brain included, carry out in order to stay alive. It includes energy use, but also maintenance, regulation and waste removal. Metabolism informs models of how our muscles work when we run, how our lungs work when we breathe, and how our immune system works when we get sick. Since the human mind has something to do with the brain, it stands to reason that metabolism should inform models of how our brain works when we think. And, indeed, most scholars nowadays tend to accept that the brain is important to understanding the mind, even if they leave it out of their models.

The brain is a quirky organ, metabolically speaking. It consumes a lot of energy compared with other parts of the human body. Though it makes up around 2 per cent of an adult’s body mass, it consumes about 20 per cent of its calories. Yet it is impressively efficient. The brain on average operates at about 20 watts – less than an incandescent lightbulb. A ‘lightbulb moment’, in other words, probably consumes less energy than an actual lightbulb.

According to one study by William Levy and Victoria Calvert of the University of Virginia, the electrical signals (or ‘spikes’) that send information use only about 3.5 watts. Building and strengthening synapses, which is how information is stored, uses about 1.3 watts. It is not entirely understood how the brain can do so much with so little, but part of the answer is evolution: organisms with more efficient brains had a selective advantage for searching for food and avoiding predators. The human mind operates under tremendous metabolic constraints.

Focusing on metabolism might seem to fly in the face of much philosophical analysis of the mind. Many philosophers set the brain aside when building their theories, freeing the mind from its substratum. One reason is the widespread acceptance of multiple realisability, a view first set out by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in the 1960s, which holds that the same mental states can be realised by different neural states. What determines a mental state is what it does, not what it’s made of. This is how an octopus could still feel pain, even if its brain is unlike ours – it’s the state that matters, not the physical substratum. Some philosophers go further, adopting John Haugeland’s notion of ‘medium independence’: if mental states are computations – a mainstream view in cognitive science – then these states are independent of the specific medium in which they are embodied. Mental states are defined by formal rules, and these same rules can be implemented in different media. The familiar analogy is the computer: the same software (the mind) can be run on different hardware (the brain). Both views reject the idea that there is a one-to-one match between the mind and the brain. They suggest that the mind can be fruitfully studied on its own terms, making metabolism irrelevant to modelling.

Yet even brain-friendly philosophers have largely disregarded brain metabolism. Patricia Churchland, who urged philosophers to learn neuroscience, co-wrote a 1988 paper that defined the aim of computational neuroscience as explaining how the brain’s signals are used ‘to represent and process information’. But the chemistry that maintains those signals was lost in this framing. The philosopher Carl Craver and colleagues stay close to the biological ground when they argue that mechanisms are ‘entities and activities organised such that they are productive of regular changes’, for example neurotransmitters binding to receptors. But here too the energy that makes those activities possible figures as a background condition rather than as part of the explanation.

We argue that metabolism constrains which models of the mind are viable. It could occur via different brain processes, or in nonbiological media like silicon-based digital computers. Whatever the medium, all these systems will be constrained by energy use, maintenance and waste removal. A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support, and studying metabolism is how we find out where that limit lies.

So the metabolic constraints on physical systems like brains cannot be ignored when modelling the mind. Rather than taking them to be firm metaphysical commitments, we should think of them as working hypotheses: great starting points, but open to revision after new research.

title: Der Pilger, der Geschichte schrieb
subtitle: Antony Beevor zeigt Rasputin als schillernde Persönlichkeit ebenso wie als historischen Faktor beim Untergang des russischen Zarenreichs.
feedText: Startseite Kultur Aktuelle Seite: Buchkritik zu »Der letzte Akt« Rasputin gilt vielen als der unheimliche Strippenzieher am Hof des letzten russischen Zaren, und eine Biografie über ihn scheint eine gute Mischung aus »Sex and Crime«, Politik und Verrat, opulent lebendem Adel und darbendem Volk zu versprechen. Das Lied »Rasputin« (1978) der Popgruppe »Boney M.«, das ihn als »Lover of the Russian Queen« betitelt, dürfte zu dieser Wahrnehmung beigetragen haben. Aber was steckt hinter all diesen Mythen, Gerüchten und Berichten über den aus Sibirien stammenden Bauern, der kaum lesen und schreiben konnte, aber einen folgenschweren Einfluss auf die Zarenfamilie und damit auf die Geschichte Russlands gewann? Der namhafte Historiker Antony Beevor beleuchtet in spannendem, erzählendem Stil all die kulturellen und politischen Umstände, die Rasputins Aufstieg ins Zentrum des Zarenreichs und vor allem ins Innerste der Familie Romanow ermöglichten. »Der letzte Akt« ist daher nicht nur für Leser interessant, die etwas über Rasputin erfahren möchten. Das Buch bietet auch tiefe Einblicke in das Russland zu Anfang des 20.

## Buchkritik zu »Der letzte Akt«

### Pilgernd zur Macht

### Rasputin als Symbol für den Niedergang der Monarchie

Startseite Kultur Aktuelle Seite: Buchkritik zu »Der letzte Akt« Rasputin gilt vielen als der unheimliche Strippenzieher am Hof des letzten russischen Zaren, und eine Biografie über ihn scheint eine gute Mischung aus »Sex and Crime«, Politik und Verrat, opulent lebendem Adel und darbendem Volk zu versprechen. Das Lied »Rasputin« (1978) der Popgruppe »Boney M.«, das ihn als »Lover of the Russian Queen« betitelt, dürfte zu dieser Wahrnehmung beigetragen haben. Aber was steckt hinter all diesen Mythen, Gerüchten und Berichten über den aus Sibirien stammenden Bauern, der kaum lesen und schreiben konnte, aber einen folgenschweren Einfluss auf die Zarenfamilie und damit auf die Geschichte Russlands gewann? Der namhafte Historiker Antony Beevor beleuchtet in spannendem, erzählendem Stil all die kulturellen und politischen Umstände, die Rasputins Aufstieg ins Zentrum des Zarenreichs und vor allem ins Innerste der Familie Romanow ermöglichten. »Der letzte Akt« ist daher nicht nur für Leser interessant, die etwas über Rasputin erfahren möchten. Das Buch bietet auch tiefe Einblicke in das Russland zu Anfang des 20. Jahrhunderts – und damit kurz vor seinem Kollaps. Pilgernd zur Macht So erfährt der – durchaus überraschte – Leser, welch große Bedeutung Rasputins Religiosität für seinen Zugang zum Adel hatte. Denn seinen Aufstieg begann er als »Strannik«, als mittelloser Pilger, der von Ort zu Ort zog. Stranniki galten als heilige Menschen, die Krankheiten heilen und zukünftige Ereignisse vorhersagen konnten. Auch in den Adelshäusern erfreuten sie sich großer Beliebtheit. Als religiöse Autorität erlangte Rasputin – trotz seines zweifelhaften Leumunds aufgrund seiner Ausschweifungen, die bis hin zu sexueller Gewalt gingen – Zugang zum innersten Kern der Zarenfamilie. Vor allem auf die Zarin Alexandra Fjodorowna hatte Rasputin ungeheuren Einfluss. Sie betrachtete ihn als weisen Freund der Familie, ohne den keine politische Entscheidung getroffen werden durfte. Bald konnte im Zarenreich nur noch ein politisches Amt besetzen, wer Rasputin gegenüber bedingungslose Loyalität zeigte. Dies geschah in einer Zeit, die für die Dynastie der Romanows auch so schon gefährlich genug war. Innenpolitisch gab es massive Unruhen aufgrund der prekären Lage der Arbeiter und Bauern, die der Erste Weltkrieg noch weiter verschlimmerte. Der Adel schwelgte im Reichtum, während Korruption und Misswirtschaft das Land zugrunde richteten. Zar Nikolaus II. war derweil von seinem eigenen Gottesgnadentum überzeugt, zeigte aber keinerlei Mitgefühl für die leidende Bevölkerung. Rasputin als Symbol für den Niedergang der Monarchie Zudem hatte sich Rasputin viele Feinde unter den russischen Adeligen gemacht, die im Zuge seines Aufstiegs an Einfluss bei Hofe verloren hatten. Auch in der Öffentlichkeit genoss Rasputin einen schlechten Ruf: Er wurde zum Symbol für Korruption, Machtmissbrauch und die Schwäche der Monarchie. Das Gerücht, dass Rasputin der Geliebte der Zarin sei, kostete Nikolaus II.

> [“An appropriately designed critical thinking class can dramatically reduce four common biases in judgment and decision making”](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2027-52606-001) — a newly published study by Michael Bishop, Adam Feltz, and Paul Conway [(previously discussed here)](https://dailynous.com/2026/02/16/crafting-a-critical-thinking-course-that-sticks-with-students-guest-post/)

title: Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA?
subtitle: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association.
feedText:
# Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA?

Skip to main content

## Why is Fox Newsobsessed with the WNBA?

Fox News

Fox News’ fixation on the league dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t consume Fox News myself.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ cable coverage of the WNBA.

The first clue came at a family gathering. A conservative relative started name-dropping WNBA players, praising superstar Caitlin Clark while parroting right-wing conspiracy theories about Black players. This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

Background graphic pulls out and plays four videos with chyron headlines: “Why does the left hate Caitlin Clark?”, “Flagrant fouls against Caitlin Clark continue”, “ WNBA suspends Thomas 1 game after punching Clark”, and “Critics say Caitlin Clark is being snubbed by the WNBA.”

The second clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, I was recommended more. That made sense. But then stories from, of all places, Fox News started appearing in my feed.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about the WNBA.

Headline after headline pitted Clark, the league’s white, straight-coded star, against other players, almost entirely Black and queer women.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about Caitlin Clark. Three headlines are pulled out: “Caitlin Clark fans unload on WNBA, Thomas after violent sequence leaves Fever star battered,” “WNBA star who hurt Caitlin Clark’s eye calls for league to take action against Trump administration policies”, and “Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese a jacka– for jealousy of Caitlin Clark in response to ESPN analyst.”

Fox News also singled out specific players, framing Angel Reese as “entitled” and “laughably bad,” despite Reese being named the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year and reaching the Finals in her third year (notably, before Clark).

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about Angel Reese. Four headlines are pulled out: “Angel Reese embarrasses herself with cringe video, needs to get a grip: WATCH”, “Why does Angel Reese get a pass for acting like an entitled brat over her dumb Caitlin Clark comment?”, “Don’t be fooled, Angel Reese was laughably bad in another blowout loss”, and “Angel Reese dangerously peddles racist conspiracy theory after WNBA coach calls her two words.”

When it comes to sports, there are, at least seemingly, facts. This team won, and this team lost. This player scored a lot of points. You would expect a lot of similar coverage. But this was different. On their website, Fox News even elevated the WNBA right alongside… literal war.

A screenshot from the Fox News home page in August 2026.

To measure just how deep this obsession ran, I turned to data.

I analyzed over 30,000 WNBA-related articles from 2019 to 2026 across Fox News (and its sports arm OutKick) against six peer outlets: the Associated Press, CBS (Sports + News), ESPN (+Andscape), The New York Times (+The Athletic), USA Today, and the Washington Post.

To see what was happening on television, I also analyzed thousands of cable news chyrons — the banners running across the bottom of the screen — from Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC (now MS NOW) dating back to 2017. See more in the methods.

on the web

### Which players get an outsized share of Fox News’ attention?

Compared with

on television

### The words used in television chyrons

Cable news chyrons, September 2017–November 1, 2026, from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye.

Let’s look at online headlines first. The center line here represents an equal balance. If Fox News and other outlets devoted the exact same percentage of their WNBA coverage to Clark, she would sit right in the middle.

A dot plot showing the share of coverage by players including Sophie Cunningham, DiJonai Carrington, Angel Reese, Caitlin Clark, Natasha Cloud, Brittney Griner, Aliyah Boston, Paige Bueckers, Alyssa Thomas, Kelsey Mitchell, A'ja Wilson, Breanna Stewart, and Napheesa Collier. The X axis ranges from 15× bigger share for other outlets (left) to equal (center) to 15× bigger share for Fox News (right).

Instead, Clark pulls a 3.5× larger share of Fox News’ WNBA headlines than she does across all other outlets combined (the further right a player is, the more heavily they over-index on Fox News).

Clark’s dot moves right to 3.5× bigger share for Fox News.

Other players get an outsized share of Fox News’ attention, too — but largely when they can be plugged into the network’s culture-war machinery.

All other players’ dots move. Sophie Cunningham, DiJonai Carrington, Angel Reese, Caitlin Clark, Natasha Cloud, and Brittney Griner have bigger shares of coverage on Fox News. Aliyah Boston has equal coverage. Paige Bueckers, Alyssa Thomas, Kelsey Mitchell, A'ja Wilson, Breanna Stewart, and Napheesa Collier have bigger shares of coverage by other outlets.

Fox News champions players who match its base. Sophie Cunningham draws 10× more headline share on the network than across other mainstream outlets, boosted by her public stance against trans inclusion in sports.

Sophie Cunningham’s dot is highlighted showing 10× bigger share of Fox News headlines.

It turns outspoken players into political lightning rods, obsessing over Natasha Cloud’s racial justice activism and Brittney Griner’s Russian imprisonment and gender identity.

srText: Natasha Cloud’s dot (3.1× Fox News) and Brittney Griner’s dot (2.1× Fox News) are highlighted, showing bigger shares of Fox News headlines.

It also inflames on-court tension by weaponizing physical play, framing Black players like Reese and DiJonai Carrington as hostile or violent toward their white counterparts.

Angel Reese’s dot (3.3× Fox News) and DiJonai Carrington’s dot (6.7× Fox News) are highlighted, showing bigger shares of Fox News headlines.

Napheesa Collier’s dot (5.2× other outlets), Gabby Williams’ dot (3.8× other outlets), Breanna Stewart’s dot (3.5× other outlets) and A’ja Wilson’s dot (2.0× other outlets) are highlighted, showing bigger shares of other outlets’ headlines.

But digital headlines are only half the picture. What happens when the lens shifts to prime-time cable?

On television, similar patterns emerge. This ternary plot maps chyron mentions across Fox News (top), CNN (bottom-left), and MSNBC (now MS NOW, bottom-right). The center marks balanced coverage; the closer a dot pulls toward a corner, the more exclusively that single network dominates the conversation.

The dot plot turns into a triangle chart of cable news chyrons, with Fox News at the top, CNN at the bottom left and MSNBC at the bottom right. Sophie Cunningham, DiJonai Carrington, Alyssa Thomas, Gabby Williams, A’ja Wilson and Natasha Cloud are in Fox News’ zone. Caitlin Clark sits on the edge of Fox News’ zone. Angel Reese, Paige Bueckers, Kelsey Mitchell, Breanna Stewart and Napheesa Collier are in CNN’s zone. Brittney Griner and Aliyah Boston are in MSNBC’s zone.

Clark hovers on the Fox News border, with the network accounting for half of her chyron mentions. She serves as an entry point for cultural grievances, especially when paired alongside players who skew even further into Fox News’ territory.

FoxCNNMSNBCFox%

- Fox share:50%
At Fox News’ top apex sits Cunningham, propelled by her public opposition to trans athletes and her reputation as Clark’s“bodyguard.” Fox News routinely pits the two Fever teammates against openly queer Black players like Carrington and Alyssa Thomas, sensationalizing fouls as “cheap shots” or malicious.

Sophie Cunningham, DiJonai Carrington and Alyssa Thomas are highlighted, all in Fox News’ zone.

FoxCNNMSNBCFox%

- Fox share:99%
- Fox share:93%
- Fox share:86%
Fox News routinely bypasses the WNBA’s top talent. The network missed obvious editorial layups: it ignored Napheesa Colliercalling out league leadership — a critique directly aligned with Fox News’ own anti-WNBA talking points — and overlooked Clark’s backcourt partner, Kelsey Mitchell, as she set the all-time single-season scoring record.

Napheesa Collier, Paige Bueckers, Breanna Stewart and Kelsey Mitchell are highlighted in CNN’s zone, and Aliyah Boston in MSNBC’s zone.

- Fox share:0%

An exception among the league's elite is five-time MVP Wilson. Long anchored in CNN territory, her dot swung sharply toward Fox News following an on-court confrontation with a fan during the 2026 playoffs, underscoring how quickly the network tunes in when athletic greatness can be recast as public conflict.

A’ja Wilson’s dot is highlighted, in Fox News’ zone.

FoxCNNMSNBCFox%

- Fox share:57%
### Fightin’ Words

Understanding Fox News’ framing means looking beyond who they cover to how they cover them.

To do that, we applied a text-analysis method aptly called “fightin’ words.” The model pinpoints words uniquely tied to a specific outlet, adjusting for corpus size while deemphasizing commonly used jargon (like “head coach”) and rare, low-signal names (like OutKick writer “Dan Dakich”).

Each term receives a measurement that is standardized as a z-score — what we’ll call a “distinctiveness score” — ranking words by how disproportionately one outlet relies on them compared to the rest.

See how Fox News’ top phrases compare across possible methods.▾RankFightin’ wordsWeighted log odds with an informative prior (z-score)Raw countTimes Fox uses the phraseRate differenceFox’s rate minus others’, per 10,000 phrasesArticle ratioArticles with the phrase, Fox / others1social mediasocial mediasocial mediaDan Dakich2white privilegewomen’s basketballwomen’s sportsstay fearless3black womenwomen’s sportswomen’s basketballpopular because4women’s sportshead coachFever staridentity politics5Fever starnational championshipcollege basketballCari Champion

on the web

### The phrases that define Fox News’ coverage

Compared with1–0 of 0

Fox News: 3,420 WNBA articles; the other outlets: 17,901, April 2023 on. Words ranked by weighted log-odds with an informative prior (Monroe et al. 2008). Tan bars are z-scores under 1.96 (a common threshold). Hover a bar for an example.

Weighted log-odds ratio with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008), using Jack Hessel's implementation, over headlines from April 2023 on. “All outlets” pools ESPN, CBS Sports, USA Today, Just Women's Sports and The Athletic, which together publish far more than Fox — so the horizontal axis, which counts both archives at once, is mostly theirs. Hover any word for the split. The shaded band is |z| < 1.96, where the difference is not distinguishable from chance.

Plotted side by side, WNBA coverage looks like two parallel universes: all other outlets on the left, Fox News on the right.

A diverging bar chart showing the two-word phrases uniquely used by other outlets (left) vs. Fox News (right).

On the left, other outlets focus on actual basketball, emphasizing game strategy with terms like points, rebounds, and free agency.

Basketball phrases are highlighted on the other outlets’ side, such as scored points, points rebounds, free agency, point guard and fourth quarter. None of Fox News’ phrases are highlighted.

Meanwhile, on the right, Fox News’ vocabulary barely touches on-court play. Its coverage is driven by social media reactions and political flashpoints, leaning heavily into conservative buzzwords like “white privilege,” “national anthem,” and “biological men.”

Four of Fox News’ phrases are highlighted: social media (its top phrase), white privilege, national anthem and biological men.

At the center of this framing sits “Fever star” Clark, whom Fox News repeatedly tethers to its conservative agenda.

“Fever star” is highlighted, the 5th phrase on Fox News’ side.

Beyond overarching themes, how are individual players framed? Stars like Clark are often framed very strategically. There is a “fight over Caitlin Clark’s soul,” as professor Kate Starbird, a misinformation researcher and former WNBA player, put it to me. Starbird and collaborators are currently tracking WNBA “outrage bait” on social media, where Clark is often a centerpiece.

When Clark entered the league in 2024, the culture-war media machinery shifted into overdrive (explore our historical network timeline below). Some commentators suggested that conservative audiences embraced Clark partly because of her background as a straight-presenting, white, Midwestern star. As Courtney M. Cox writes in Double Crossover, “It is essential to highlight how basketball, racialized as a Black sport, still privileges whiteness, especially in media coverage and endorsement.”

Starbird notes that Clark isn’t a “stable” figure for the conservative or liberal media. With a few exceptions, Clark is talked about more than she talks — at least off the court, and not to the refs.

To map how those narratives take shape, we applied the distinctiveness model to specific grammatical roles: how players are described, how their play is characterized, what actions they take, and what is done to them.

Sometimes this is Fox News editorializing directly — “Carrington is a dirty player.” Other times, it captures quoted speech or players defending themselves (“DiJonai Carrington sent a message to fans who think she plays ‘dirty.’”) But with “ragebait” media, the distinction collapses: by highlighting Carrington’s claim that she’s not a dirty player, they incite their audience to insist that she is.

Because these player-specific descriptors appear less frequently overall, some carry lower distinctiveness scores that fall below traditionally used thresholds (indicated by tan bars below). They are included because even words used a handful of times (or fewer) can speak volumes. Fox News characterizing Angel Reese’s play as “pathetic” just three times carries immense weight, especially when no other outlets used the word to describe a player (outside quoted speech) across tens of thousands of articles.

You can see the divergent framing even with specific incidents. When Carrington accidentally poked Clark in the eye during a playoff game, The New York Times (via The Athletic) treated the collision as incidental basketball contact. Fox News, meanwhile, opened with a dramatic scene of Carrington sticking her “long fingernail” into Clark’s eye, burying Clark’s comments about intentionality paragraphs later.

vs.New York Times

### “Rejecting” Identity Politics

While Fox News vociferously rejects “identity politics” in WNBA coverage, they’ve accused outlets like ESPN, USA Today, and The Athletic of being “racial idolaters” and generally injecting left-wing politics about race, gender, and sexuality into their reporting.

Laura Ingraham and Clay Travis, the founder of OutKick, discuss a USA Today column that suggested some of Clark’s fans were racist.

Here’s the irony: Fox News talks more about race, gender, and identity in the WNBA than any other outlet. This year they’ve mentioned race or racial politics in 23% of their WNBA articles, and LGBTQ+ topics in 34%, far more than any other outlet.

Does Fox News simply write more opinion-oriented coverage, while the other outlets stick to sports? I don’t think so, at least not entirely.

For one thing, this comparison includes any opinion pieces or off-court coverage from other outlets, and Fox News does cover actual game play. But the amount of editorializing in Fox News’ reporting is telling in its own right. Few, if any, outlets write about the WNBA quite so much through a cultural and political lens.

A closer look reveals the formula behind that framing.

### Fox News’ framing increasingly relies on “Us vs. Them”

Fox News’ WNBA playbook wasn’t built overnight. In 2019, the network covered the league like everyone else: which is to say, barely at all. Coverage was sparse, mostly confined to the occasional box score, trade note, or injury update, with a few sporadic pieces on players’ activism or politics, like Natasha Cloud’s.

That shifted during the 2020 COVID bubble season when players turned their activism into tangible political power, mobilizing to help unseat Dream co-owner and GOP Senator Kelly Loeffler. Hostility hardened in 2022, during Griner’s imprisonment in Russia. Fox News commentators and conservative politicians often reinforced one another’s framing of the prisoner swap as a weak concession for an “unpatriotic” athlete.

How Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC split coverage of race in television chyrons

Across mainstream outlets, coverage of race peaked in 2020 during the height of the Black Lives Matter movement. That summer, WNBA players led high-profile demonstrations inside the bubble, walking off the court during the national anthem and wearing “Say Her Name” shirts on national television.

But unlike other outlets, Fox News’ coverage of race didn’t fall off after 2020. Instead, it rebounded and was reframed when Clark entered the league in 2024.

Fox News’ most distinctive race-related phrases aren't about civil rights or systemic equity. They are combative culture-war slogans: “race bullies,” “race idolaters,” and even “race war.”

### Fox News dramatically accelerated its coverage of LGBTQ+ topics in the last year

on television

How Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC split coverage of LGBTQ+ topics in television chyrons

Fox News’ obsessions with race, gender, and the LGBTQ+ community, especially trans women, are intimately connected — a dynamic long unpacked by Black, feminist, and queer scholars through intersectional concepts like “misogynoir” (coined by Moya Bailey) and “transmisogynoir.”

Fox News routinely highlights white players who conform to traditional conventions of femininity — like Cunningham, Kelsey Plum, and Cameron Brink — while denigrating Black players who do not, advancing an ideal of straight, white, femme womanhood. Drawing these boundaries has only one obvious end: hating women, including trans women.

Cunningham reinforced this framing with anti-trans remarks of her own. While she told ESPN that she “got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans” and clarified that “I never once said that,” she repeated conservative anti-trans talking points about “protect[ing] young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men.”

She later doubled down on those comments. And right-wing politicians and anti-trans advocates worldwide rallied around her, including Vice President J.D. Vance, J.K. Rowling, and Jennifer Sey.

Vice President J.D. Vance praises Sophie Cunningham on Fox News, August 2026.

Trans women’s participation in the WNBA has become a non-stop Fox News preoccupation. On television, they spent more than 13 hours discussing the WNBA in summer 2026 alone. It’s worth repeating: no transgender players are currently in the league.

In our analysis of chyrons from Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC, Fox News was responsible for 96% of the usage of the word “trans” and 90% for “transgender,” totaling over 200 uses.

As Fox News pundit Jesse Watters recently said on air regarding Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve wearing a “Trans Kids Belong” shirt: “We have to do this again, really? Someone wore a t-shirt at a WNBA game? This isn’t a news story…. We don’t even cover the NBA. Why are we covering the WNBA?”

### Fox News particularly focuses on fouls and “protecting” Clark

on the web

on television

How Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC split coverage of fouls in television chyrons

One particularly powerful right-wing WNBA narrative — which arguably ties both implicit racism and transphobia together — is about fouls.

From the moment Clark entered the league, conservatives have pushed a story that other players are purposely targeting her on the court, often suggesting it’s because she is white. While Clark has faced real physicality — and calls for better officiating were widespread — the narrative of racialized persecution was pure political spin.

Letter from Republicans to the WNBA commissioner

The Republicans cite, as evidence, the fact that “Clark has been hip-checked, poked in the eye, and struck in the throat during games.” It was an almost verbatim echo of Fox News, who spent months repeating those exact words across more than 200 articles fretting about the need to “protect” Clark.

That fixation on “protecting” Clark easily merged with another familiar right-wing narrative. By casting the WNBA as a hostile environment in need of cultural rescue, commentators tapped into the exact same “protect women and children” playbook long weaponized against trans women.

### This coverage matters

It’s tempting to dismiss this coverage as drivel. But unfortunately, it matters.

Fox News

Fox News anchors a media pipeline connecting prolific right-wing blogs and fringe online content farms directly to Republican politicians, including Donald Trump, who fawned over Cunningham’s looks and castigated the league to loud boos at rallies in the lead-up to the 2026 midterms.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ cable coverage of the WNBA. Two videos of Trump talking about the WNBA are pulled out.

As their own host Jesse Watters openly said on air, Fox News doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball. They are exploiting world-class athletes as lucrative ragebait. And it’s working, at least as a business strategy: in August 2026, Fox’s OutKick hit a record 13 million visitors.

Three Fox News clips are pulled out: The Five on a WNBA coach’s “Trans kids belong” T-shirt aimed at Sophie Cunningham, The Big Weekend Show on WNBA Finals ratings amid national anthem drama, and Joe Concha on Cunningham’s post-election message going viral.

The issue isn’t that women’s basketball is being made political — sports are, and have always been, political. The danger is how quickly manufactured panic hardens into policy: Even as the 2026 midterms signaled a broader pushback against anti-trans rhetoric, voters in several states, including my home state of Washington, passed measures restricting transgender students from participating on sports teams that align with their gender identity.

We can’t let the WNBA be weaponized as a Trojan horse for anti-trans politics, or bigotry of any kind. The version of the league peddled by conservative media, the “ragebait W,” is unrecognizable to anyone actually watching the games. So let’s change the channel.

As Roxane Gay argued, the WNBA must match its players’ progressive courage — welcoming trans women while fiercely shielding its athletes from “bad-faith attacks, death threats, harassment, and other racial animus.”

The background switches like a TV changing channels and now shows roughly 40 examples of other outlets’ coverage of the WNBA. Four clips are pulled out: Gabby Williams in an interview, CBS Evening News on the WNBA and players reaching a historic deal, CNN on average WNBA salaries that could rise to over $1 million, and Layshia Clarendon speaking to Andscape.

The W is built different. Inclusivity is in its DNA: from the community in the stands, to beloved non-binary and Black-coded mascots, to the players' relentless push for equity on and off the court. And the basketball is electric. In this pivotal moment of the league’s growth, we need to see the outrage machine for what it is and push back, lest we all get played.

# Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA?

Skip to main content

## Why is Fox Newsobsessed with the WNBA?

Fox News

Fox News’ fixation on the league dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t consume Fox News myself.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ cable coverage of the WNBA.

The first clue came at a family gathering. A conservative relative started name-dropping WNBA players, praising superstar Caitlin Clark while parroting right-wing conspiracy theories about Black players. This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

Background graphic pulls out and plays four videos with chyron headlines: “Why does the left hate Caitlin Clark?”, “Flagrant fouls against Caitlin Clark continue”, “ WNBA suspends Thomas 1 game after punching Clark”, and “Critics say Caitlin Clark is being snubbed by the WNBA.”

The second clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, I was recommended more. That made sense. But then stories from, of all places, Fox News started appearing in my feed.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about the WNBA.

Headline after headline pitted Clark, the league’s white, straight-coded star, against other players, almost entirely Black and queer women.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about Caitlin Clark. Three headlines are pulled out: “Caitlin Clark fans unload on WNBA, Thomas after violent sequence leaves Fever star battered,” “WNBA star who hurt Caitlin Clark’s eye calls for league to take action against Trump administration policies”, and “Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese a jacka– for jealousy of Caitlin Clark in response to ESPN analyst.”

Fox News also singled out specific players, framing Angel Reese as “entitled” and “laughably bad,” despite Reese being named the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year and reaching the Finals in her third year (notably, before Clark).

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about Angel Reese. Four headlines are pulled out: “Angel Reese embarrasses herself with cringe video, needs to get a grip: WATCH”, “Why does Angel Reese get a pass for acting like an entitled brat over her dumb Caitlin Clark comment?”, “Don’t be fooled, Angel Reese was laughably bad in another blowout loss”, and “Angel Reese dangerously peddles racist conspiracy theory after WNBA coach calls her two words.”

When it comes to sports, there are, at least seemingly, facts. This team won, and this team lost. This player scored a lot of points. You would expect a lot of similar coverage. But this was different. On their website, Fox News even elevated the WNBA right alongside… literal war.

A screenshot from the Fox News home page in August 2026.

To measure just how deep this obsession ran, I turned to data.

I analyzed over 30,000 WNBA-related articles from 2019 to 2026 across Fox News (and its sports arm OutKick) against six peer outlets: the Associated Press, CBS (Sports + News), ESPN (+Andscape), The New York Times (+The Athletic), USA Today, and the Washington Post.

To see what was happening on television, I also analyzed thousands of cable news chyrons — the banners running across the bottom of the screen — from Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC (now MS NOW) dating back to 2017. See more in the methods.

### Fightin’ Words

Understanding Fox News’ framing means looking beyond who they cover to how they cover them.

That shifted during the 2020 COVID bubble season when players turned their activism into tangible political power, mobilizing to help unseat Dream co-owner and GOP Senator Kelly Loeffler. Hostility hardened in 2022, during Griner’s imprisonment in Russia. Fox News routinely highlights white players who conform to traditional conventions of femininity — like Cunningham, Kelsey Plum, and Cameron Brink — while denigrating Black players who do not, advancing an ideal of straight, white, femme womanhood. Drawing these boundaries has only one obvious end: hating women, including trans women.

Cunningham reinforced this framing with anti-trans remarks of her own. While she told ESPN that she “got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans” and clarified that “I never once said that,” she repeated conservative anti-trans talking points about “protect[ing] young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men.”

She later doubled down on those comments. And right-wing politicians and anti-trans advocates worldwide rallied around her, including Vice President J.D. Vance, J.K. Rowling, and Jennifer Sey.

Vice President J.D. Vance praises Sophie Cunningham on Fox News, August 2026.

In our analysis of chyrons from Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC, Fox News was responsible for 96% of the usage of the word “trans” and 90% for “transgender,” totaling over 200 uses.

As Fox News pundit Jesse Watters recently said on air regarding Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve wearing a “Trans Kids Belong” shirt: “We have to do this again, really? Someone wore a t-shirt at a WNBA game? This isn’t a news story…. We don’t even cover the NBA. Why are we covering the WNBA?”

One particularly powerful right-wing WNBA narrative — which arguably ties both implicit racism and transphobia together — is about fouls.

From the moment Clark entered the league, conservatives have pushed a story that other players are purposely targeting her on the court, often suggesting it’s because she is white. While Clark has faced real physicality — and calls for better officiating were widespread — the narrative of racialized persecution was pure political spin.

Letter from Republicans to the WNBA commissioner

The Republicans cite, as evidence, the fact that “Clark has been hip-checked, poked in the eye, and struck in the throat during games.” It was an almost verbatim echo of Fox News, who spent months repeating those exact words across more than 200 articles fretting about the need to “protect” Clark.

That fixation on “protecting” Clark easily merged with another familiar right-wing narrative. By casting the WNBA as a hostile environment in need of cultural rescue, commentators tapped into the exact same “protect women and children” playbook long weaponized against trans women.

### This coverage matters

It’s tempting to dismiss this coverage as drivel. But unfortunately, it matters.

Fox News

Fox News anchors a media pipeline connecting prolific right-wing blogs and fringe online content farms directly to Republican politicians, including Donald Trump, who fawned over Cunningham’s looks and castigated the league to loud boos at rallies in the lead-up to the 2026 midterms.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ cable coverage of the WNBA. Two videos of Trump talking about the WNBA are pulled out.

As their own host Jesse Watters openly said on air, Fox News doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball. They are exploiting world-class athletes as lucrative ragebait. And it’s working, at least as a business strategy: in August 2026, Fox’s OutKick hit a record 13 million visitors.

Three Fox News clips are pulled out: The Five on a WNBA coach’s “Trans kids belong” T-shirt aimed at Sophie Cunningham, The Big Weekend Show on WNBA Finals ratings amid national anthem drama, and Joe Concha on Cunningham’s post-election message going viral.

The issue isn’t that women’s basketball is being made political — sports are, and have always been, political. The danger is how quickly manufactured panic hardens into policy: Even as the 2026 midterms signaled a broader pushback against anti-trans rhetoric, voters in several states, including my home state of Washington, passed measures restricting transgender students from participating on sports teams that align with their gender identity.

We can’t let the WNBA be weaponized as a Trojan horse for anti-trans politics, or bigotry of any kind. The version of the league peddled by conservative media, the “ragebait W,” is unrecognizable to anyone actually watching the games. So let’s change the channel.

As Roxane Gay argued, the WNBA must match its players’ progressive courage — welcoming trans women while fiercely shielding its athletes from “bad-faith attacks, death threats, harassment, and other racial animus.”

The background switches like a TV changing channels and now shows roughly 40 examples of other outlets’ coverage of the WNBA. Four clips are pulled out: Gabby Williams in an interview, CBS Evening News on the WNBA and players reaching a historic deal, CNN on average WNBA salaries that could rise to over $1 million, and Layshia Clarendon speaking to Andscape.

The W is built different. Inclusivity is in its DNA: from the community in the stands, to beloved non-binary and Black-coded mascots, to the players' relentless push for equity on and off the court. And the basketball is electric. In this pivotal moment of the league’s growth, we need to see the outrage machine for what it is and push back, lest we all get played.

## Why is Fox Newsobsessed with the WNBA?

Fox News

Fox News’ fixation on the league dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t consume Fox News myself.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ cable coverage of the WNBA.

The first clue came at a family gathering. A conservative relative started name-dropping WNBA players, praising superstar Caitlin Clark while parroting right-wing conspiracy theories about Black players. This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

Background graphic pulls out and plays four videos with chyron headlines: “Why does the left hate Caitlin Clark?”, “Flagrant fouls against Caitlin Clark continue”, “ WNBA suspends Thomas 1 game after punching Clark”, and “Critics say Caitlin Clark is being snubbed by the WNBA.”

The second clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, I was recommended more. That made sense. But then stories from, of all places, Fox News started appearing in my feed.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about the WNBA.

Headline after headline pitted Clark, the league’s white, straight-coded star, against other players, almost entirely Black and queer women.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about Caitlin Clark. Three headlines are pulled out: “Caitlin Clark fans unload on WNBA, Thomas after violent sequence leaves Fever star battered,” “WNBA star who hurt Caitlin Clark’s eye calls for league to take action against Trump administration policies”, and “Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese a jacka– for jealousy of Caitlin Clark in response to ESPN analyst.”

Fox News also singled out specific players, framing Angel Reese as “entitled” and “laughably bad,” despite Reese being named the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year and reaching the Finals in her third year (notably, before Clark).

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about Angel Reese. Four headlines are pulled out: “Angel Reese embarrasses herself with cringe video, needs to get a grip: WATCH”, “Why does Angel Reese get a pass for acting like an entitled brat over her dumb Caitlin Clark comment?”, “Don’t be fooled, Angel Reese was laughably bad in another blowout loss”, and “Angel Reese dangerously peddles racist conspiracy theory after WNBA coach calls her two words.”
